CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTION TODAY conscientious objection around the world Too many countries still fail to recognise people’s right to refuse, because of moral or religious convictions, to serve in armed forces. Here are some stories from some of these countries. ARMENIA Jehovah’s Witnesses are forbidden by their religion to serve in an army or carry weapons. It was not until 2004 that the Armenian government at last introduced laws for conscientious objection and the option of doing alternative civilian duties instead of serving in the army. Until then, Jehovah’s Witnesses who refused call-up to military service were described as ‘persistent draft-dodgers’ and ‘evaders of active military service’. This meant that they could be prosecuted in a criminal court – evasion of service is listed as a crime with a penalty of up to 3 years in prison. Though they had the chance to put their case in court, and later in courts of appeal, most were sentenced to a year or more in prison – though they may have already spent quite a long time in prison waiting for their case to come up. Some have served longer sentences, often in labour camps. Even with the new law, which allows for alternative service for those whose claim to be conscientious objectors is accepted, arrests for ‘draft-dodging’ were still being made, and many who were already in prison had not been freed. ERITREA In Eritrea the law is that men and women between the ages of 18 and 40 must do 18 months of military service, a stretch which in reality usually ends up being much longer. There is no right to conscientious objection. The government has deployed military police throughout the country using roadblocks, street sweeps, and house-to-house searches to find deserters and draft evaders. Amnesty International reported in November 2004 that since 1998 the Eritrean military had been rounding up and arresting thousands of young men and others suspected of evading military conscription. These arrests had recently been stepped up. Many young men and women have fled from the country as refugees in order to avoid conscription. ‘Soldiers go into offices, houses, stop cars, taxis, buses, and ask for identity cards,’ said one young man. The report described how some people recently arrested were now in an army prison. Conditions there were harsh, with severe overcrowding, not much food and little sanitation. Some, it was said, had been forced to sleep outside in very cold weather without blankets or shoes. Prisoners had no access either to their families or to lawyers. There were also reports that the army has used severe physical punishment to force objectors, including some Jehovah's Witnesses, to perform military service. In some instances, authorities were said to have arrested or detained (for hours or even days) a number of people, including pregnant women, children under 18, and citizens of other countries – even though they were not liable for call-up, and even if they had documents proving they had already done military service or were exempt from it.

FINLAND
Compulsory military service in Finland lasts for up to a year. The Finnish government requires that anyone who refuses to do military service must do alternative civilian service instead. But alternative service lasts twice as long as military service and so amounts to a form of punishment. Conscientious objectors who have refused to do alternative service have been sent to prison.

Finland 2004: tunnelling into prison where conscientious objectors are imprisoned.

GERMANY Compulsory military service in Germany usually lasts 9 months, and applies to all men between the ages of 18 and 23. (Women may also volunteer if they choose.) Alternative service lasts 10 months or more. In 2003 two ‘total objectors’ (people who refuse not only compulsory military service but also the alternative service which is also run by the military) were arrested: they had been called up, and though they dutifully turned up at their barracks they refused to obey any military orders. The usual fate of German total objectors has been to spend up to about 3 months under military arrest. Then they are tried for criminal disobedience in civilian law courts. GREECE In Greece men serve a year’s compulsory military service, though this may be reduced if the government’s establishment of a professional army system proceeds as planned. The right to conscientious objection was not recognised in Greece until 1997. The case of one conscientious objector caused War Resisters International to launch a campaign to support him. He first declared himself a CO in 1992. In the following years he was imprisoned 3 times and taken to court 12 times. In 1998 he applied for status as a CO under the new 1997 law, but though he was accepted he was also called up for alternative service – for a term over 7 times longer than his military service would have been. He refused to do alternative service. In 1999 he was arrested again and sentenced to 4 years in prison. He appealed against the sentence, which was eventually suspended. But then he was called up again! At the end of 2004 he was once more arrested, tried and sentenced to two and a half years in prison. Campaigners point out that he had now been tried and punished twice for the same ‘offence’, and should be released. ISRAEL Military service in Israel is compulsory for men, and can last up to 3 years. Service of up to 2 years is also compulsory for women unless they have married before call-up age. Some men and women belonging to ethnic and religious groups are exempt from call-up. Israel’s ‘refuseniks’ – soldiers who have refused to obey orders to harass or kill Palestinian civilians – have become famous. In recent years a few have managed to get exemption from military service. They had to succeed in convincing the military authorities that they were pacifists. In the case of women, Israel’s conscription law allows exemption to those who are pacifists or who have a strict ‘religious family lifestyle’. But in practice being a pacifist (but not committed to a religious life) has not been enough for the military courts to agree to grant exemption. At the end of 2004 the legal rights of women COs were still unclear and uncertain. :: > Noam Bahat's testimony RUSSIAN FEDERATION Russian men serve a compulsory 2 years in the armed forces. A law allowing for conscientious objection came into operation on January 1 2004. According to this law, alternative civilian service lasts much longer: 3 and a half years. It was reported that by the autumn 616 people had applied for alternative service. The problem, however, is finding alternative service jobs for them to do. Some have been doing welfare work (in nursing homes, for example). But others have been sent to military construction sites and factories, which is not civilian service. SERBIA & MONTENEGRO Alternative civilian service was introduced here in December 2003. Problems quickly cropped up, because no civilian service work had been organised. COs who refused unarmed work in the armed forces were threatened with imprisonment. In at least one case, a CO who was called up for unarmed work agreed to start, but refused some military tasks he was asked to do. Eventually he refused to return to his unit at all, and returned to civilian life with a suspended prison sentence hanging over him. It was reported that over 12,000 young men applied for CO status after alternative service became an option. Over 6,000 were in alternative service posts by the end of 2004. SOUTH KOREA Compulsory military service here is for 2 years. The Korean Supreme Court and the Constitutional Court have denied that conscientious objection is a human right, and say that ‘national security’ is in any case more important than an individual’s human rights. Two COs took their case to the United Nations in 2004: they claim that their right to conscientious objection is implied in the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, which upholds ‘freedom of thought, conscience and religion’. When the outcome of this move is known, it will have significance for COs worldwide. Meanwhile COs continued to be arrested and imprisoned. Some object to call-up because of their Buddhist religion. Some have objected in particular to the deployment of South Korean troops in Iraq. Yet others are pacifists, and some of these are active protesters in the pacifist cause, working with organisations such as World Without War and Amnesty International, or in liberal political groups, or through publications and the press. Some have protested by going on hunger strike. One conscript who declared his conscientious objection to taking part in the war in Iraq was arrested at the end of 2003. His defence was that the South Korean constitution banned wars of aggression. The judge told him that the USA was friendly towards South Korea and therefore must be supported in every way. The CO was sentenced to 2 years in prison, later shortened by 6 months. SWITZERLAND Switzerland has an army 200,000 strong. Military service is compulsory for men and lasts nearly a year. Women have the same training but service is voluntary. Conscientious objectors can choose 450 days of civilian service – much longer than military service – instead. A law on conscientious objection was passed in 1992, but allows very few reasons for claiming conscientious objection. This has meant that some COs have not even applied for CO status, but have found other ways out. There have been reports of successful evasion of military service for medical or other reasons. Some men have obtained dismissal from military training. One objector declared himself a CO in 1996, but his application for alternative service was turned down and he was called up in 1999. He refused to serve and was sentenced to 5 months in prison. Here the conditions in which he was kept grew steadily worse. It was claimed that he was a security threat. His windows were sealed, he was refused contact with any other prisoners, his mail was kept from him, and visits were rarely allowed – and then only to people vetted by the prison authorities. The prison manager said that this was to prevent publicity. The CO began a hunger strike in protest. TURKEY Military service is compulsory for almost all men between the ages of 20 and 40, and lasts for at least 6 months. Refusing to serve has been illegal, punishable by imprisonment. Conscientious objection has not been accepted. There have been grim reports of harsh prison conditions and even torture. One particular conscientious objector was arrested in 1996, charged with disobeying orders. He spent 2 and a half years in prison. Here he met another prisoner. This man had been imprisoned for serious crime and facing a likely life sentence; he was also a supporter of fascism and contemptuous of conscientious objection. But gradually the two men began to talk. The CO (whose case was accepted in 2004 for examination by the European Court of Human Rights) remembers: ‘Although our thoughts were in conflict, he began to respect me, followed by a kind of friendship. He tried more and more to understand my principles. We began to discuss ethics, religion, history, nationalism, psychology and so on.’ When the now ex-fascist was released under an amnesty in 2002, he too declared himself to be a conscientious objector.

| | Today part of | [Zimbabwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe "Zimbabwe") | | 1. **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_ref-mon_1-0)** The government recognised Queen [Elizabeth II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_II "Elizabeth II") as the official [head of state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_heads_of_state_of_Zimbabwe#Unrecognised_monarchy_\(1965%E2%80%931970\) "List of heads of state of Zimbabwe") from 1965 to 1970. The highest official of Rhodesia held the title "[Officer Administering the Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administrator_of_the_government#Rhodesia "Administrator of the government")" (OAtG) as he acted in lieu of the official [Governor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Southern_Rhodesia "Governor of Southern Rhodesia"), who remained at his post but was ignored. After Rhodesia became a republic in March 1970, the President replaced the OAtG as the highest official and the Governor returned to London. | **Rhodesia** ( [_roh-DEE\-zhə_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key"), [_roh-DEE\-shə_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key");[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-2) [Shona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shona_language "Shona language"): _Rodizha_), officially the **Republic of Rhodesia** from 1970,[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-3)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-4) was an [unrecognised](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unrecognised_state "Unrecognised state") country in [Southern Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Africa "Southern Africa") that existed from 1965 to 1979. Rhodesia served as the _[de facto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_facto "De facto")_ [successor state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Succession_of_states "Succession of states") to the [British colony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_colony "Crown colony") of [Southern Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia "Southern Rhodesia") following a [unilateral declaration of independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence "Rhodesia's Unilateral Declaration of Independence") issued by the ruling white-minority government. Throughout this fourteen-year period, Rhodesia faced internal conflict and political unrest. Following the [Lancaster House Agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancaster_House_Agreement "Lancaster House Agreement") in 1979, the territory returned to British political control and then subsequently gained internationally recognised independence as [Zimbabwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe "Zimbabwe") in 1980. The rapid [decolonisation of Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decolonisation_of_Africa "Decolonisation of Africa") in the late 1950s and early 1960s alarmed a significant proportion of Southern Rhodesia's white population. In an effort to delay the transition to [black majority rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No_independence_before_majority_rule "No independence before majority rule"), the predominantly white Southern Rhodesian government issued its own [Unilateral Declaration of Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence "Rhodesia's Unilateral Declaration of Independence") (UDI) from the United Kingdom on 11 November 1965. The new nation, identified simply as Rhodesia, initially sought [recognition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diplomatic_recognition "Diplomatic recognition") as an autonomous [realm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_realm "Commonwealth realm") within the [Commonwealth of Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_Nations "Commonwealth of Nations"), but reconstituted itself as a republic in 1970. Following the declaration of independence in 1965,[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-5) the [United Nations Security Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council "United Nations Security Council") passed a resolution that called upon all states not to grant recognition to Rhodesia. Two [African nationalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_nationalism "African nationalism") parties, the [Zimbabwe African People's Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_African_People%27s_Union "Zimbabwe African People's Union") (ZAPU) and [Zimbabwe African National Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_African_National_Union "Zimbabwe African National Union") (ZANU), launched an armed insurgency against the government upon UDI, sparking the [Rhodesian Bush War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_Bush_War "Rhodesian Bush War"). Growing war weariness, diplomatic pressure, and an extensive trade embargo imposed by the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations") prompted Rhodesian prime minister [Ian Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Smith "Ian Smith") to [concede to majority rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internal_Settlement "Internal Settlement") in 1978. However, [elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1979_Rhodesian_general_election "1979 Rhodesian general election") and a multiracial [provisional government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_Rhodesia "Zimbabwe Rhodesia"), with Smith succeeded by moderate [Abel Muzorewa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abel_Muzorewa "Abel Muzorewa"), failed to appease international critics or halt the war. By December 1979, Muzorewa had secured an [agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancaster_House_Agreement "Lancaster House Agreement") with ZAPU and ZANU, allowing Rhodesia to briefly revert to colonial status pending [new elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_Southern_Rhodesian_general_election "1980 Southern Rhodesian general election") under British supervision. ZANU secured an electoral victory in 1980, and the country achieved internationally recognised independence in April 1980, as Zimbabwe. A [landlocked](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landlocked_country "Landlocked country") nation, Rhodesia was bordered by [Botswana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Botswana "Botswana") ([Bechuanaland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bechuanaland_Protectorate "Bechuanaland Protectorate"): British protectorate until 1966) to the southwest, [Mozambique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People%27s_Republic_of_Mozambique "People's Republic of Mozambique") (as a [Portuguese province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Mozambique "Portuguese Mozambique") until 1975) to the east, [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa") to the south, and [Zambia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zambia "Zambia") ([Northern Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Rhodesia "Northern Rhodesia") until 1964) to the northwest. From 1965 to 1979, Rhodesia was one of two independent states on the African continent governed by a [white minority of European descent and culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Zimbabweans "White Zimbabweans"), the other being South Africa. Rhodesia's largest cities were [Salisbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harare "Harare") (its capital city, now known as Harare) and [Bulawayo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulawayo "Bulawayo"). Prior to 1970, the [unicameral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unicameralism "Unicameralism") Legislative Assembly was predominantly white, with a small number of seats reserved for black representatives. Following the declaration of a republic in 1970, this was replaced by a [bicameral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicameralism "Bicameralism") [Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_Rhodesia "Parliament of Rhodesia"), with a [House of Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Assembly_/(Zimbabwe/) "House of Assembly (Zimbabwe)") and a [Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_of_Zimbabwe "Senate of Zimbabwe"). The bicameral system was retained in Zimbabwe after 1980. Aside from its [racial franchise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_Rhodesia#1961_constitution "Politics of Rhodesia"), Rhodesia observed a [Westminster system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_system "Westminster system") inherited from the United Kingdom, with a [president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Rhodesia "President of Rhodesia") acting as ceremonial head of state, while a [prime minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Rhodesia "Prime Minister of Rhodesia") headed the [Cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_Rhodesia "Cabinet of Rhodesia") as head of government. The official name of the country, according to the constitution adopted concurrently with the UDI in November 1965, was Rhodesia, which derives from [Cecil Rhodes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Rhodes "Cecil Rhodes"). This was not the case under [British law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom_law "United Kingdom law"), however, which considered the territory's legal name to be [Southern Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia "Southern Rhodesia"), the name given to the country in 1898 during the [British South Africa Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_South_Africa_Company "British South Africa Company")'s [administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Company_rule_in_Rhodesia "Company rule in Rhodesia") of [the Rhodesias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia_/(region/) "Rhodesia (region)"), and retained by the [self-governing colony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-governing_colony "Self-governing colony") of Southern Rhodesia after the end of company rule in 1923.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-rowland251-6) This naming dispute dated back to October 1964, when [Northern Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Rhodesia "Northern Rhodesia") became independent from the UK and concurrently changed its name to [Zambia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zambia "Zambia"). The Southern Rhodesian colonial government in [Salisbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harare "Harare") felt that in the absence of a "Northern" Rhodesia, the continued use of "Southern" was superfluous. It passed legislation to become simply Rhodesia, but the British government refused to approve this on the grounds that the country's name was defined by British legislation, so could not be altered by the colonial government. Salisbury went on using the shortened name in an official manner nevertheless,[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-palley742743-7) while the British government continued referring to the country as Southern Rhodesia. This situation continued throughout the UDI period.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-rowland251-6) The shortened name was used by many people including the British government in the House of Commons. Until after the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War") the landlocked British possession of [Southern Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia "Southern Rhodesia") was not developed as an indigenous African territory, but rather as a unique state that reflected its [multiracial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiracialism "Multiracialism") character.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-duignan1986-8) This situation certainly made it very different from other lands that existed under colonial rule, as many Europeans had arrived to make permanent homes, populating the towns as traders or settling to farm the most productive soils.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-areahandbook-9)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-taylor2006-10) In 1922, faced with the decision to join the [Union of South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_of_South_Africa "Union of South Africa") as a fifth province or accept nearly full internal autonomy, the electorate cast its vote against South African integration.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-11)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-12)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-13) In view of the outcome of the referendum, the territory was annexed by the United Kingdom on 12 September 1923.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-14)[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-15)[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-ReferenceA-16)[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-17) Shortly after annexation, on 1 October 1923, the first constitution for the new Colony of Southern Rhodesia came into force.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-ReferenceA-16)[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-18) Under this constitution, Southern Rhodesia was given the right to elect its own thirty-member [legislature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesian_Legislative_Assembly "Southern Rhodesian Legislative Assembly"), [premier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Rhodesia "Prime Minister of Rhodesia"), and cabinet—although the British government retained a formal veto over measures affecting natives and dominated foreign policy.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-19)[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-20)[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-21) Over the course of the next three decades, Southern Rhodesia experienced a degree of economic expansion and industrialisation almost unrivaled in sub-Saharan Africa.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Barber-22) Its natural abundance of mineral wealth—including large deposits of [chromium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium "Chromium") and [manganese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese "Manganese")—contributed to the high rate of conventional economic growth.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Barber-22) However, most colonies in Africa, even those rich in natural resources, experienced difficulty in achieving similar rates of development due to a shortage of technical and managerial skills.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Barber-22) Small, rotating cadres of colonial civil servants who possessed little incentive to invest their skills in the local economy were insufficient to compensate for this disadvantage.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Barber-22) Southern Rhodesia had negated the issue by importing a skilled workforce directly from abroad in the form of its disproportionately large European immigrant and expatriate population.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Barber-22) For example, in 1951 over 90% of white Southern Rhodesians were engaged in what the British government classified as "skilled occupations", or professional and technical trades.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Barber-22) This made it possible to establish a diversified economy with a strong manufacturing sector and iron and steel industries, and circumvent the normal British protectionist policy of supporting domestic industry in the metropole while discouraging industry in the colonies abroad.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-duignan1986-8)[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-23) As the white population increased, so did capital imports, especially in the wake of the Second World War.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Barber-22) This trend, too, stood in sharp contrast to most other colonial territories, which suffered a major capital deficit due to revenues simply being repatriated to the metropole, leaving little capital to be invested locally.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-World-24) The considerable investment made by white Rhodesians in the economy financed the development of Southern Rhodesia's export industries as well as the infrastructure necessary to integrate it further with international markets.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Barber-22) In August 1953, Southern Rhodesia merged with [Northern Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Rhodesia "Northern Rhodesia") and [Nyasaland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyasaland "Nyasaland"), the two other British Central African territories, to form the [Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland "Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland") – a loose association that placed defence and economic direction under a central government but left many domestic affairs under the control of its constituent territories.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-weitzer1990-25) As it began to appear that decolonisation was inevitable and indigenous black populations were pressing heavily for change,[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-duignan1986-8) the federation was dissolved at the end of December 1963.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-26)[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-27) ### Unilateral Declaration of Independence (1965) \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rhodesia&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: Unilateral Declaration of Independence (1965)")\] Although prepared to grant formal independence to Southern Rhodesia (now Rhodesia), the [British government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_government "British government") had adopted a policy of _[no independence before majority rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No_independence_before_majority_rule "No independence before majority rule")_ (NIBMR), dictating that colonies with a significant, politically active population of European settlers would not receive independence except under conditions of [majority rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Majority_rule "Majority rule").[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-28)[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-29)[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-30) White Rhodesians balked at the premise of NIBMR; many felt they had a right to absolute political control, at least for the time being, despite their relatively small numbers.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-weitzer1990-25)[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-31) They were also disturbed by the chaos of the post-colonial political transitions occurring in other African nations at the time, such as the [Democratic Republic of the Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Republic_of_the_Congo "Democratic Republic of the Congo").[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-SmithGB-32)[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Spikes-33) A vocal segment of the white populace was open to the concept of gradually incorporating black Rhodesians into civil society and a more integrated political structure in theory, although not without qualification and equivocation.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-West-34) A greater degree of social and political equality, they argued, was acceptable once more black citizens had obtained higher educational and vocational standards.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-West-34) The second faction in the white community was wholly unwilling to concede the principle, much less the practice, of equality to the black population.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-West-34) Both groups remained opposed to majority rule in the near future.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-West-34) However, once Rhodesia had been introduced as a topic for discussion in international bodies, extension of the status quo became a matter of concern to the British government, which perceived the scrutiny as a serious embarrassment to the United Kingdom.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-areahandbook-9) After the federation was dissolved in December 1963, British Prime Minister Sir [Alec Douglas-Home](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alec_Douglas-Home "Alec Douglas-Home") insisted that preconditions on independence talks hinge on what he termed the "five principles" – unimpeded progress to majority rule, assurance against any future legislation decidedly detrimental to black interests, "improvement in the political status" of local Africans, an end to official [racial discrimination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racial_discrimination "Racial discrimination"), and a political settlement that could be "acceptable to the whole population".[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-35)[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-36)[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-37) [Harold Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Wilson "Harold Wilson") and his incoming [Labour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_/(UK/) "Labour Party (UK)") government took an even harder line on demanding that these points be legitimately addressed before a timetable for independence could be set.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-areahandbook-9) In 1964, growing white dissatisfaction with the ongoing negotiations played a major role in the ousting of [Winston Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winston_Field "Winston Field") as [Prime Minister of Southern Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Southern_Rhodesia "Prime Minister of Southern Rhodesia"). Field was succeeded by [Ian Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Smith "Ian Smith"), chairman of the conservative [Rhodesian Front Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_Front_Party "Rhodesian Front Party") and an outspoken critic of any immediate transition to majority rule.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-38)[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-39)[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-40) Smith, the colony's first Rhodesian-born leader, soon came to personify resistance to liberals in British government and those agitating for change at home.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-areahandbook-9) In September 1964, Smith visited [Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon "Lisbon"), where Portuguese prime minister [António de Oliveira Salazar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ant%C3%B3nio_de_Oliveira_Salazar "António de Oliveira Salazar") promised him "maximum support" if he should declare independence.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Onslow-41) Aside from a common interest in maintaining security ties in southern Africa, Salazar expressed a great deal of anger at Britain's refusal to support Portugal during the [Indian annexation of Goa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annexation_of_Goa "Annexation of Goa") in 1961, admonishing Smith not to trust the British government.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Onslow-41) A [Rhodesian Trade Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_mission_in_Lisbon "Rhodesian mission in Lisbon") was opened in Lisbon in order to co-ordinate breaking the anticipated sanctions in the event of a unilateral declaration of independence later that year, which encouraged Smith not to compromise.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Onslow-41) In its turn, the Rhodesian Trade Office in Lisbon functioned as a _de facto_ embassy and caused tension with London, which objected to Rhodesia conducting its own foreign policy.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Onslow-41) As land-locked Rhodesia bordered the [Portuguese colony of Mozambique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Mozambique "Portuguese Mozambique"), Salazar's promise of "maximum support" from [Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estado_Novo_/(Portugal/) "Estado Novo (Portugal)") in breaking the anticipated sanctions gave Smith more grounds for self-confidence in his talks with London.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Onslow-41) Smith ruled out acceptance for all five of the British principles as they stood,[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-42) implying instead that Rhodesia was already legally entitled to independence—a claim that was overwhelmingly endorsed by the predominantly white electorate in a [referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesian_independence_referendum,_1964 "Southern Rhodesian independence referendum, 1964").[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-43)[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-44) Emboldened by the results of this referendum and the subsequent general election, the Rhodesian government threatened to declare independence without British consent. [Harold Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Wilson "Harold Wilson") countered by warning that such an irregular procedure would be considered [treasonous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treason "Treason"), although he specifically rejected using armed force to quell a rebellion by English "kith and kin", or white Rhodesians of predominantly British descent and origin, many of whom still possessed sympathies and family ties to the United Kingdom.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-45)[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-guardian.co.uk-46) Wilson's refusal to consider a military option further encouraged Smith to proceed with his plans. Talks quickly broke down, and final efforts in October to achieve a settlement floundered; the Smith government remained unwilling to accept the five principles of independence, and the British government argued it would settle for nothing less.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-areahandbook-9) [![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/a/a9/Udi2-rho.jpg/250px-Udi2-rho.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Udi2-rho.jpg) [Ian Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Smith "Ian Smith") signing the Unilateral Declaration of Independence On 11 November 1965 the [Cabinet of Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_Rhodesia "Cabinet of Rhodesia") issued a [unilateral declaration of independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence "Rhodesia's Unilateral Declaration of Independence") (UDI).[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-duignan1986-8)[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-raft-47)[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-blackfire-48) The UDI was immediately denounced as an "act of rebellion against the Crown" in the United Kingdom, and Wilson promised that the illegal action would be short-lived.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-49)[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-50) However, given its self-governing status Rhodesia had no longer been within the United Kingdom's direct sphere of influence for some time, and the façade of continued British rule was rendered a constitutional fiction by UDI.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-weitzer1990-25) In light of these circumstances, Wilson quickly realised his ability to assert direct leverage over the incumbent Rhodesian government was limited.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-weitzer1990-25) On 12 October 1965, the [United Nations General Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_General_Assembly "United Nations General Assembly") had noted the repeated threats of the Rhodesian authorities "to declare unilaterally the independence of Southern Rhodesia, in order to perpetuate minority rule", and called upon Wilson to use all means at his disposal (including military force) to prevent the Rhodesian Front from asserting independence.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-51) After UDI was proclaimed, UN officials branded the Rhodesian government as an "illegal racist minority regime"[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-52) and called on member states to voluntarily sever economic ties with Rhodesia, recommending [sanctions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_sanctions "International sanctions") on petroleum products and military hardware.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-areahandbook-9) In December 1966, the UN further iterated that these sanctions were mandatory, and member states were explicitly barred from purchasing Rhodesian export goods, namely tobacco, chromium, copper, asbestos, sugar, and beef.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-areahandbook-9) The British government, having already adopted extensive sanctions of its own, [dispatched](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beira_Patrol "Beira Patrol") a [Royal Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Navy "Royal Navy") squadron to monitor oil deliveries in the port of [Beira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beira,_Mozambique "Beira, Mozambique") in Mozambique, from which a strategic pipeline ran to [Umtali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mutare "Mutare") in Rhodesia. The warships were to deter "by force, if necessary, vessels reasonably believed to be carrying oil destined for (Southern) Rhodesia".[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-53)[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-gowlland-debbas1990-54) Some Western nations, such as Switzerland and [West Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Germany "West Germany"), which were not UN member states, continued to conduct business openly with Rhodesia – the latter remained the Smith government's largest trading partner in Western Europe until 1973, when it was admitted to the UN.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-areahandbook-9) Japan remained the chief recipient of Rhodesian exports outside the African continent, and [Iran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pahlavi_Iran "Pahlavi Iran") also supplied oil to Rhodesia in violation of the embargo.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-55) Portugal served as a conduit for Rhodesian goods, which it exported through Mozambique with false [certificates of origin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Certificate_of_origin "Certificate of origin").[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-okoth2006-56) South Africa, too, refused to observe the UN sanctions.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-57)[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-58) In 1971, the [Byrd Amendment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byrd_Amendment_/(1971/) "Byrd Amendment (1971)") was passed in the United States, permitting American firms to go on importing Rhodesian chromium and nickel products as normal.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-meredith-59) Despite the poor showing of sanctions, Rhodesia found it nearly impossible to obtain diplomatic recognition abroad. In 1970, the United States declared it would not recognise UDI "under \[any\] circumstances".[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-a-60) South Africa and Portugal, Rhodesia's largest trading partners, also refused to extend diplomatic recognition, and did not open embassies in the Rhodesian capital, [Salisbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harare "Harare"), preferring to conduct diplomatic activities through "accredited representatives".[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-google13-61) This allowed the South African and Portuguese governments to maintain they were continuing to respect British sovereignty while also accepting the practical authority of the Smith administration.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-google257-62) Initially, the Rhodesian state retained its pledged loyalty to Queen [Elizabeth II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_II "Elizabeth II"), recognising her as Queen of Rhodesia.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-areahandbook-9) When Smith and Deputy Prime Minister [Clifford Dupont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_Dupont "Clifford Dupont") visited Sir [Humphrey Gibbs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humphrey_Gibbs "Humphrey Gibbs"), the [Governor of Southern Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Southern_Rhodesia "Governor of Southern Rhodesia"), to formally notify him of the UDI, Gibbs condemned it as an act of treason. After Smith formally announced the UDI on the radio, Governor Gibbs used his [reserve power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reserve_power "Reserve power") to dismiss Smith and his entire cabinet from office, on orders from the [Colonial Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonial_Office "Colonial Office") in [Whitehall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitehall "Whitehall"). However, Gibbs was unable to take any concrete actions to bring about a return to lawful colonial government. Rhodesian ministers simply ignored his notices, contending that UDI had made his office obsolete. Even so, Gibbs continued to occupy his [official residence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Official_residence "Official residence"), [Government House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_House,_Harare "State House, Harare"), in Salisbury until 1970, when he finally left Rhodesia, following the declaration of a republic.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Age-63) He had effectively been superseded before then; the Smith government stated that if the Queen did not appoint a Governor-General, it would name Dupont as "[Officer Administering the Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Officer_Administering_the_Government "Officer Administering the Government")".[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-strips-64) Smith had intended to have Dupont named Governor-General, but Queen Elizabeth II would not even consider this advice.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-65) With few exceptions, the international community backed Whitehall's assertion that Gibbs was the Queen's only legitimate representative, and hence the only lawful authority in Rhodesia. In September 1968, the [Appellate Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appellate_court "Appellate court") of the [High Court of Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Court_of_Rhodesia "High Court of Rhodesia") ruled that Ian Smith's administration had become the _de jure_ government of the country, not merely the _de facto_ one.[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Beadle-66) To support his decision, Chief Justice Sir [Hugh Beadle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Beadle "Hugh Beadle") used several statements made by [Hugo Grotius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugo_Grotius "Hugo Grotius"), who maintained that there was no way that a nation could rightly claim to be governing a particular territory – if it was waging a war against that territory. Beadle argued that due to Britain's economic war against Rhodesia, she could not (at the same point) be described as _governing_ Rhodesia.[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-67)[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-68) The ruling set the precedent that despite the UDI, the incumbent Smith government "could lawfully do anything its predecessors could lawfully have done".[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-legalitylaw-69) A Salisbury commission chaired by prominent lawyer W.R. Waley was appointed to study constitutional options open to the Rhodesian authorities as of April 1968, including on the topic of majority rule, but reopening negotiations with the British on a settlement was ruled out early on.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-weitzer1990-25)[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-70) The Waley Commission found that in practical as well as legal terms, "Europeans must surrender any belief in permanent European domination", pointing out that minority rule was not permanently sustainable.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-areahandbook-9) However, Waley also testified that majority rule was not desirable immediately.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-areahandbook-9) Talks aimed at easing the differences between Rhodesia and the United Kingdom were carried out aboard Royal Navy vessels once in December 1966 and again in October 1968.[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-71)[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-72)[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-73) Both efforts failed to achieve agreement, although Harold Wilson added a sixth principle to the five he had previously enunciated: "it would be necessary to ensure that, regardless of race, there was no oppression of the majority by the minority or of \[any\] minority by the majority." Rhodesian resolve stiffened following a failure to reach a new settlement, with more radical elements of the Rhodesian Front calling for a republican constitution.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-areahandbook-9) During a [two-proposition referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_constitutional_referendum,_1969 "Rhodesian constitutional referendum, 1969") held in 1969, the proposal for severing all remaining ties to the British Crown passed by a majority of 61,130 votes to 14,327.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-areahandbook-9) Rhodesia declared itself a republic on 2 March 1970. Under the new constitution, a president served as ceremonial head of state, with the prime minister nominally reporting to him.[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-74) Some in the Rhodesian government had hoped in vain that the declaration of a republic would finally prompt other nations to grant recognition.[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-75) The years following Rhodesia's UDI saw an unfolding series of economic, military, and political pressures placed on the country that eventually brought about majority rule, a totality of these factors rather than any one the reason for introducing change.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-frontiersmen-76) In 2005, a conference at the [London School of Economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_School_of_Economics "London School of Economics") that discussed Rhodesia's independence concluded that UDI was sparked by an existing racial conflict complicated by [Cold War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War "Cold War") intrigues.[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-b-77) Critics of UDI maintained that Ian Smith intended to safeguard the privileges of an entrenched colonial ruling class at the expense of the impoverished black population.[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-c-78) Smith defended his actions by claiming that the black Rhodesian majority was too inexperienced at the time to participate in the complex administrative process of what was, by contemporary African standards, a reasonably industrialised state.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-SmithGB-32) At large, UDI further hardened the white population's attitudes towards majority rule and relations with the UK.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-raft-47) A significant majority of white Rhodesian residents were either British immigrants or of British ancestry, and many held a special affection for the British Empire.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-raft-47) However, the UK's refusal to grant them independence on their terms further confirmed their opposition to a political settlement on British terms, and fed their negative attitudes towards British interference in Rhodesian politics at large.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-raft-47) In the years prior to UDI, white Rhodesians increasingly saw themselves as beleaguered and threatened, perpetually insecure and undermined by the metropole, unable to rely on anybody but themselves.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-SmithGB-32) The policy of "No independence before majority rule" transformed the white community's relationship with the UK and increased its suspicions of the British government's untrustworthiness and duplicity in colonial affairs, especially since the latter had adopted NIBMR as a formal policy - the very circumstance UDI was carried out to avoid, and which white Rhodesians had struggled to resist since the onset of decolonisation.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-SmithGB-32) Black nationalist parties reacted with outrage at UDI, with one ZANU official stating, "for all those who cherish freedom and a meaningful life, UDI has set a collision course that cannot be altered. 11 November 1965 \[has\] marked the turning point of the struggle for freedom in that land from a constitutional and political one to primarily a military struggle."[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-blackfire-48) It would, however, be several years before the nationalists adopted armed struggle as their primary strategy for obtaining political power.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-blackfire-48) Violent tactics at this time were intended to create opportunities for [external intervention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interventionism_/(politics/) "Interventionism (politics)"), either by the international community or the British government, rather than seriously undermine the Rhodesian security forces.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-blackfire-48) Because Rhodesian exports were generally competitive and had previously been entitled to preferential treatment on the British market, the former colony did not recognise the need for escalating the pace of [diversification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diversification_/(marketing_strategy/) "Diversification (marketing strategy)") before independence. Following the UDI, however, Rhodesia began to demonstrate that it had the potential to develop a greater degree of economic [self-sufficiency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-sufficiency "Self-sufficiency").[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-SmithGB-32)[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-79) After the Rhodesian Front began introducing incentives accorded to domestic production, industrial output expanded dramatically. A rigid system of countermeasures enacted to combat sanctions succeeded in blunting their impact for at least a decade.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-areahandbook-9) Over the next nine years, Rhodesian companies, spiting the [freezing of their assets and blocking of overseas accounts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_asset_recovery "International asset recovery"), also perfected cunning techniques of sanctions evasion through both local and foreign subsidiaries, which operated on a clandestine trade network.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-areahandbook-9) From 1968 until 1970, there was virtually no further dialogue between Rhodesia and the UK. In a [referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_constitutional_referendum,_1969 "Rhodesian constitutional referendum, 1969") in 1969, white voters approved a new constitution and the establishment of a republic, thereby severing Rhodesia's last links with the British Crown, duly declared in March 1970. This changed immediately after the election of [Edward Heath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Heath "Edward Heath"), who reopened negotiations.[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-racewar-80) Smith remained optimistic that Heath would do his utmost to remedy Anglo-Rhodesian relations, although disappointed that he continued to adhere publicly to the original "five principles" proposed by Alec Douglas-Home, now [foreign secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_State_for_Foreign_and_Commonwealth_Affairs "Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs"). In November 1971, Douglas-Home renewed contacts with Salisbury and announced a proposed agreement that would be satisfactory to both sides – it recognised Rhodesia's 1969 constitution as the legal frame of government, while agreeing that gradual legislative representation was an acceptable formula for unhindered advance to majority rule.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-areahandbook-9) Nevertheless, the new settlement, if approved, would also implement an immediate improvement in black political status, offer a means to terminate racial discrimination, and provide a solid guarantee against retrogressive constitutional amendments.[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-81) Implementation of the proposed settlement hinged on popular acceptance, but the Rhodesian government consistently refused to submit it to a universal referendum.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-areahandbook-9) A twenty four-member commission headed by an eminent jurist, [Lord Pearce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Pearce,_Baron_Pearce "Edward Pearce, Baron Pearce"), was therefore tasked with ascertaining [public opinion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_opinion "Public opinion") on the subject.[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-historyps-82) In 1972, the commission began interviewing interest groups and sampling opinions – although concern was expressed over the widespread [apathy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_apathy "Political apathy") encountered.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-SmithGB-32) According to the commission, whites were in favour of the settlement, and Rhodesians of [Coloured](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloured "Coloured") or Asian ancestry generally pleased, while the black response to the settlement's terms was resoundingly negative.[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-racewar-80)[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-83) As many as thirty black Rhodesian chiefs and politicians voiced their opposition, prompting Britain to withdraw from the proposals on the grounds of the commission's report.[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-historyps-82) #### Early militant activity \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rhodesia&action=edit§ion=7 "Edit section: Early militant activity")\] As early as 1960, [minority rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minority_rule "Minority rule") in Southern Rhodesia was already being challenged by a rising tide of [political violence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_violence "Political violence") led by black African nationalists such as [Joshua Nkomo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Nkomo "Joshua Nkomo") and [Ndabaningi Sithole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ndabaningi_Sithole "Ndabaningi Sithole"). A sustained period of civil unrest between 1960 and 1965 further polarised relations between the government and the increasingly militant black nationalists.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-blackfire-48) After their public campaigns were initially suppressed, many black nationalists believed that negotiation was completely incapable of meeting their aspirations. Petrol bombings by politicised radicals became increasingly common, with the _Zimbabwe Review_ observing in 1961, "for the first time home-made petrol bombs were used by freedom fighters in Salisbury against settler establishments."[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-84) Between January and September 1962, nationalists detonated 33 bombs and were implicated in 28 acts of arson, and 27 acts of sabotage against communications infrastructure.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-blackfire-48) The nationalists also murdered a number of black Rhodesians who were accused of collaboration with the security forces.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-blackfire-48) Nkomo's party, the [Zimbabwe African People's Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_African_People%27s_Union "Zimbabwe African People's Union") (ZAPU) announced that year that it had formed a military wing, the [Zimbabwe People's Revolutionary Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_People%27s_Revolutionary_Army "Zimbabwe People's Revolutionary Army") (ZIPRA) and "the decision to start bringing in arms and ammunition and to send young men away for sabotage training" had already been implemented.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-blackfire-48) As early as 1960, ZAPU's predecessor, the National Democratic Party (NDP), had established informal contacts with the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union") and [Czechoslovakia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czechoslovak_Socialist_Republic "Czechoslovak Socialist Republic"), and discussed the possibility of obtaining military training in Eastern Europe for its members.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Hot-85) In July 1962, Nkomo visited Moscow and discussed plans for a ZAPU-led armed uprising in Rhodesia.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Hot-85) He made formal requests for Soviet funding and arms for ZIPRA, explaining that "for these purposes ZAPU needs arms, explosives, revolvers...the party also needs money to bribe persons who guard important installations, to carry out sabotage".[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Hot-85) The Soviets agreed to supply ZAPU with limited funds beginning in 1963, and increased its level of financial support after UDI.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Hot-85) In 1963, ZIPRA also made its first formal request to the Soviet Union for military training.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Hot-85) The Soviets began training ZIPRA militants in guerrilla warfare in early 1964.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Hot-85) Nkomo's public endorsement of a violent strategy confirmed white politicians' opposition to ZAPU and fed their negative attitudes towards black nationalists at large.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-blackfire-48) In response to the formation of ZIPRA, the Rhodesian government [banned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ban_/(law/) "Ban (law)") ZAPU, driving that party's supporters underground.[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-crisis-86) It also passed draconian security legislation restricting the right to assembly and granting the security forces broad powers to crack down on suspected political subversives.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-blackfire-48) For the first time, the [death sentence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_punishment "Capital punishment") was also introduced for any act of politically inspired terrorism which involved arson or the use of explosives.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-areahandbook-9) The emergence of guerrilla warfare and acts of urban insurrection by the black nationalist parties in Rhodesia allowed racial politics to be elevated into an issue of law and order in white Rhodesian public discourse. To Smith and his government, black nationalists were stateless dissidents whose primary motives were not political, but crime and perpetuating lawlessness; for example, Smith preferred to describe the insurgents as "gangsters" in his commentary.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-SmithGB-32) The use of weapons and explosives sourced from communist states by the black nationalists also disguised the racial dynamics of the conflict, allowing white Rhodesians to claim that they were targets of Soviet-directed communist agitators rather than a domestic political movement.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-frontiersmen-76) Smith and his supporters perceived themselves as collective defenders of the traditional values of the [British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire "British Empire") against the twin threats of international communism, manifested through the Soviet Union's support for black nationalist militants, and the social and political decadence of the West.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-raft-47) Often repeated appeals to the Christian heritage of their pioneer ancestors in "defending the [free world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_world "Free world")" and sustaining "Western civilisation" reflected these beliefs.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-raft-47) This was hardly an unusual opinion among white minorities in Southern Africa at the time; a dossier compiled by United States intelligence officials on the topic found that: > many \[southern African\] whites....believe that the current social and political ferment throughout the continent is communist inspired and managed; that it would be no problem without communist instigation. They point to materiel and training provided by communist countries to insurgency groups operating against white minority governments in southern Africa. They see foreign-based black liberation groups operating against the Portuguese, Rhodesians, and South Africans as the spearhead of a communist thrust into southern Africa.[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Volk-87) ZAPU's attempts to implement its armed struggle were hamstrung by a factional split within the party between 1962 and 1963. A number of ZAPU dissidents rejected Nkomo's authority and formed their own organisation, the [Zimbabwe African National Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_African_National_Union "Zimbabwe African National Union") (ZANU), with Ndabaningi Sithole as its president and [Robert Mugabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe "Robert Mugabe") as its general secretary.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Hot-85) By August 1964, ZANU was banned by the Rhodesian government as well, which cited widespread acts of violent intimidation attributed to its members.[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-88) ZANU's agenda was left-wing and [pan-Africanist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pan-Africanism "Pan-Africanism"); it demanded a one-party state with majority rule and the abolition of private property.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-areahandbook-9) Ethnic tensions also exacerbated the split: ZANU recruited almost solely from the [Shona-speaking peoples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shona_people "Shona people") of Rhodesia.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Hot-85) Its chief support base was the rural peasantry in the [Mashonaland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mashonaland "Mashonaland") countryside.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-areahandbook-9) ZAPU did retain Shona members, even among its senior leadership following the split.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Hot-85) However, thereafter it recruited predominantly from the [Ndebele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ndebele_people "Northern Ndebele people") ethnic group.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-frontiersmen-76) Due to ZAPU's close relationship with the Soviet Union, ZANU found itself ostracised by the Soviet bloc but soon found a new ally in the [People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People%27s_Republic_of_China "People's Republic of China").[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Hot-85) Its political ideology was somewhat more influenced by the principles of [Maoism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maoism "Maoism") than ZAPU, and a sympathetic Chinese government soon agreed to furnish weapons and training for ZANU's own war effort.[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-MWM-89) After UDI, ZANU formed its own military wing, the [Zimbabwe African National Liberation Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_African_National_Liberation_Army "Zimbabwe African National Liberation Army") (ZANLA).[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-frontiersmen-76) While ZANLA and ZIPRA both planned for an armed struggle against the Rhodesian government, their respective leadership disagreed on the means of conducting the insurgency. ZIPRA favoured Soviet thinking, placing an emphasis on acquiring sophisticated weaponry in the hopes of winning a conventional battle like the [Viet Minh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viet_Minh "Viet Minh") at [Dien Bien Phu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Dien_Bien_Phu "Battle of Dien Bien Phu").[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-frontiersmen-76) ZANLA placed greater emphasis on the politicisation of the local populace in the areas it operated, and favoured a more irregular style of warfare.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-frontiersmen-76) [![Image 7](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a6/Scoutwithgun.jpg/250px-Scoutwithgun.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Scoutwithgun.jpg) Rhodesian soldier interrogating villagers in late 1977 at gunpoint. This photograph would become one of the most enduring images of the [Bush War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_Bush_War "Rhodesian Bush War"). In early April 1966, two groups of ZANLA insurgents recently trained at a Chinese military facility in [Nanjing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanjing "Nanjing") crossed into Rhodesia from Zambia, having been issued vague instructions to sabotage important installations and kill white farmers.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-blackfire-48) Five were arrested by the Rhodesian security forces almost immediately.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-blackfire-48) Another seven initially evaded capture and planned to destroy an [electric pylon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electricity_pylon "Electricity pylon") near [Sinoia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinhoyi "Chinhoyi").[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-blackfire-48) Their explosive charges failed to detonate and were discovered by the [Rhodesian Security Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_Security_Forces "Rhodesian Security Forces"), who tracked the insurgents to a nearby ranch on 28 April.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-blackfire-48) All seven were cornered and killed after a brief firefight; this event is considered to be the first engagement of the [Rhodesian Bush War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_Bush_War "Rhodesian Bush War").[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-military-90)[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-91) The action at Sinoia has been commemorated by supporters of the guerrillas since as "_Chimurenga Day_", and occupies a place of pride in ZANU hagiography.[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-MWM-89) In August 1967, a large and better-equipped column of almost seventy ZIPRA insurgents infiltrated Rhodesia from Zambia, bolstered by recruits from an allied South African militant organisation, [uMkhonto we Sizwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UMkhonto_we_Sizwe "UMkhonto we Sizwe") (MK).[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-MWM-89) The insurgents failed to cultivate prior contacts with the local populace, which immediately informed on their presence to Rhodesian officials. Within the month, the [Rhodesian police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_South_Africa_Police "British South Africa Police") and army had launched a counteroffensive codenamed [Operation Nickel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Nickel "Operation Nickel"), killing forty-seven insurgents, capturing another twenty, and driving the survivors across the border into Botswana. An even larger ZIPRA column of over a hundred insurgents was intercepted in early 1968 and annihilated by the security forces.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-frontiersmen-76) A third ZIPRA incursion attempt in July 1969 met with similarly catastrophic results.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-frontiersmen-76) Thereafter, ZIPRA abandoned the notion of attempting to infiltrate the country with large groups of insurgents equipped only with small arms; it limited itself to more irregular forms of warfare until it could stockpile enough heavy weaponry to mount a major conventional invasion.[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-MWM-89) For its part, the ZANLA leadership criticised ZIPRA's continued fixation with winning a major conventional engagement, arguing that the failed incursions demonstrated the futility of engaging the Rhodesian military in the type of pitched battles in which it held an indisputable advantage.[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-MWM-89) ZIPRA's failure to obtain support from the locals was also noted, and ZANLA began implementing a long-term covert politicisation programme to cultivate civilian support throughout its future area of operations.[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-MWM-89) ### Military and political escalation (1972–1976) \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rhodesia&action=edit§ion=8 "Edit section: Military and political escalation (1972–1976)")\] By December 1972, ZANLA had cached arms and established a vast underground network of informants and supporters in northeastern Rhodesia.[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-MWM-89) As a result of the erosion of Portuguese authority in Mozambique's border provinces due to the [Mozambican War of Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mozambican_War_of_Independence "Mozambican War of Independence"), ZANLA was also able to establish external sanctuaries there.[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-MWM-89) It was also in the process of cultivating a military alliance with the leading black nationalist movement in Mozambique, the [Front for the Liberation of Mozambique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Front_for_the_Liberation_of_Mozambique "Front for the Liberation of Mozambique") (FRELIMO).[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-MWM-89) On 21 December, a group of ZANLA insurgents under [Rex Nhongo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rex_Nhongo "Rex Nhongo") crossed into Rhodesia from Mozambique and [raided an isolated commercial farm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attack_on_Altena_Farm "Attack on Altena Farm").[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-frontiersmen-76) In the successive months, this attack was followed by a succession of raids on white farmers throughout the northeastern districts of the country and resulted in several casualties among the security forces.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-frontiersmen-76) The propaganda value of these raids, coupled with the success of ZANLA's politicisation campaign, denied intelligence to the security forces and furnished more recruits for the insurgents.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-frontiersmen-76) In response, the Rhodesian security forces began coordinating operations in Mozambique with the [Portuguese Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Army "Portuguese Army") to intercept ZANLA insurgents before they could cross the border.[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Minter-92) The practical alliances between ZIPRA and MK, and later ZANLA and FRELIMO, prompted Rhodesia to look increasingly towards South Africa and Portugal for active assistance.[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Volk-87) Rhodesian politicians frequently reminded officials in the other two nations of common security interests based on the similarity of their restive internal situations.[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Volk-87) They saw strong parallels between their nation's position of being threatened by black nationalist insurgencies and the Portuguese predicament with FRELIMO in Mozambique, as well as to a lesser extent the insurgencies in South Africa and [South West Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_West_Africa "South West Africa").[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Volk-87) Under the auspices of the [Alcora Exercise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcora_Exercise "Alcora Exercise"), the three countries' bureaucracies began routinely sharing information and seeking common diplomatic positions.[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Volk-87) Lieutenant General [Alan Fraser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_%27Pop%27_Fraser "Charles 'Pop' Fraser"), a senior strategist in the [South African Defence Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_Defence_Force "South African Defence Force") wrote in 1970, "there can be no doubt in any of our minds that we have a common enemy: we, i.e. Portugal, the RSA and Rhodesia. Unless we are to lay ourselves open to the possibility of defeat in detail, we must fight this enemy jointly—if not simultaneously."[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Volk-87) Nevertheless, aside from intelligence-sharing and some limited coordination on the operational level in Mozambique, the Portuguese could offer Rhodesia little decisive assistance. Portuguese military resources in Mozambique were preoccupied with FRELIMO and somewhat depleted by a decade of war, and little could be spared to assist a foreign ally.[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Volk-87) Rhodesia expected far more from South Africa, which possessed far greater military resources and infinitely more diplomatic influence abroad.[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Volk-87) After the [Carnation Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnation_Revolution "Carnation Revolution") and the end of Portuguese rule in Mozambique in 1975, it was no longer viable for the Smith regime to sustain white [minority rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minority_rule "Minority rule") indefinitely. By this time, even South Africa's [John Vorster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Vorster "John Vorster") had come to this view. While Vorster was unwilling to make concessions to his own country's black people, he concluded that white minority rule was not sustainable in a country where black people outnumbered white people 22:1.[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-impression-93) In 1976, there were 270,000 Rhodesians of European descent and six million Africans.[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-94) International business groups involved in the country (e.g. [Lonrho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lonrho "Lonrho")) transferred their support from the Rhodesian government to black nationalist parties. Business leaders and politicians feted Nkomo on his visits to Europe. ZANU also attracted business supporters who saw the course that future events were likely to take.[\[94\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-95) Funding and arms support provided by supporters, particularly from the Soviet Union and its allies in the latter 1970s, allowed both ZIPRA and the ZANLA to acquire more sophisticated weaponry, thereby increasing the military pressure that the guerrillas were able to place on Rhodesia. Until 1972, containing the guerrillas was little more than a police action.
