Even as late as August 1975 when Rhodesian government and black nationalist leaders met [at Victoria Falls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_Falls_Conference_/(1975/) "Victoria Falls Conference (1975)") for negotiations brokered by South Africa and Zambia, the talks never got beyond the procedural phase.[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-96) Rhodesian representatives made it clear they were prepared to fight an all out war to prevent majority rule.[\[96\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-97) However, the situation changed dramatically after the end of Portuguese colonial rule in Mozambique in 1975. Rhodesia now found itself almost entirely surrounded by hostile states and even South Africa, its only real ally, pressed for a settlement. > Having let slip one chance after another of reaching an accommodation with more moderate black leaders, Rhodesia's whites seem to have made the tragic choice of facing black nationalism over the barrel of a gun rather than the conference table. The downhill road toward a race war in Rhodesia is becoming increasingly slippery with blood. At this point, ZANU's alliance with FRELIMO and the porous border between Mozambique and eastern Rhodesia enabled large-scale training and infiltration of ZANU/ZANLA fighters. The governments of Zambia and Botswana were also emboldened sufficiently to allow resistance movement bases to be set up in their territories. Guerrillas began to launch operations deep inside Rhodesia, attacking roads, railways, economic targets and isolated security force positions, in 1976.[\[98\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-99) [![Image 8](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/0/0c/Rhodesian_Army_recruitment_Bush_War_1976.png/250px-Rhodesian_Army_recruitment_Bush_War_1976.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rhodesian_Army_recruitment_Bush_War_1976.png) A Rhodesian servicewoman taking aim with her [Browning Hi-Power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Browning_Hi-Power "Browning Hi-Power") [9×19mm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/9%C3%9719mm "9×19mm") [semi-automatic pistol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semi-automatic_pistol "Semi-automatic pistol"); from a 1976 army recruitment poster The government adopted a [strategic hamlets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategic_hamlet "Strategic hamlet") policy of the kind used in [Malaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malayan_Emergency#Comparisons_with_Vietnam "Malayan Emergency") and [Vietnam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_War "Vietnam War") to restrict the influence of insurgents over the population of rural areas. Local people were forced to relocate to protected villages (PVs) which were strictly controlled and guarded by the government against rebel atrocities. The protected villages were compared by the guerrillas to [concentration camps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concentration_camps "Concentration camps"). Some contemporary accounts claim that this interference in the lives of local residents induced many of them who had previously been neutral to support the guerrillas.[\[99\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-100) The war degenerated into rounds of increasing brutality from all three parties involved (ZANU and ZAPU, and the Rhodesian Army). Mike Subritzky, a former [New Zealand Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Army "New Zealand Army") ceasefire monitor in Rhodesia, in 1980 described the war as "both bloody and brutal and brought out the very worst in the opposing combatants on all three sides."[\[100\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-101) A major problem for the Rhodesian state in fighting the Bush War was always a shortage of manpower.[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Brownell-102): 601  Of the 3,000 white men [liable for conscription](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conscription_in_Rhodesia "Conscription in Rhodesia") in 1973, only about 1,000 reported when called-up.[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Brownell-102): 601  In February 1978, the Rhodesian Army stated it needed a minimum of 1,041 men to continue combat operations, and of those called up, only 570 reported for duty while the rest chose to move to South Africa.[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Brownell-102): 601  White emigration increased as the state called up more and more men to fight in the war, creating a vicious circle, which gradually limited the capacity of the Rhodesian state to continue the war.[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Brownell-102): 602  In order to stop white emigration, the Smith government brought in a law in 1975 forbidding Rhodesian citizens from holding foreign currency, but the law was widely flouted.[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Brownell-102): 604  In order to encourage white emigration, the guerrillas of ZANU and ZAPU followed a strategy of attacking anything and everything that was of economic value across the country in order to force the state to call up more men, and of killing white civilians.[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Brownell-102): 606  Killing Rhodesian white citizens tended to have an "echo effect" as the ZANU and ZAPU had each estimated that for one white citizen killed, it caused about 20 to leave Rhodesia.[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Brownell-102): 606 ### End of the Bush War \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rhodesia&action=edit§ion=9 "Edit section: End of the Bush War")\] [![Image 9](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/69/RhodesiaAllies1965.png/250px-RhodesiaAllies1965.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:RhodesiaAllies1965.png) [![Image 10](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d9/RhodesiaAllies1975-en.svg/250px-RhodesiaAllies1975-en.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:RhodesiaAllies1975-en.svg) The geographical situation in 1965 (left, on UDI) and 1975 (right, after the independence of Mozambique and Angola from Portugal). Green: Rhodesia; purple: friendly nations; orange: hostile states; grey: neutral countries Rhodesia began to lose vital economic and military support from South Africa, which, while sympathetic to the white minority government, never accorded it diplomatic recognition. The South African government placed limits on the fuel and munitions they supplied to the Rhodesian military. They also withdrew the personnel and equipment that they had previously provided to aid the war effort, though covert military support continued.[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-news.bbc.co.uk-103) In 1976, the South African government and [United States governments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_government "United States government") worked together to place pressure on Smith to agree to a form of majority rule. In response to the initiative of [United States Secretary of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_State "United States Secretary of State") [Henry Kissinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Kissinger "Henry Kissinger"), in 1976 Ian Smith accepted the principle of black majority rule within two years.[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-news.bbc.co.uk-103) The Rhodesians now offered more concessions, but those concessions, focused on reaching an "internal settlement" with moderate black leaders, were insufficient to end the war. At the time, some Rhodesians said the still embittered history between the British-dominated Rhodesia and the [Afrikaner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afrikaner "Afrikaner")\-dominated South Africa partly led the South African government to withdraw its aid to Rhodesia. Ian Smith said in his memoirs that even though many white South Africans supported Rhodesia, South African Prime Minister [John Vorster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Vorster "John Vorster")'s policy of [détente](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C3%A9tente "Détente") with the black African states ended up with Rhodesia being offered as the "sacrificial lamb" to buy more time for South Africa. Other observers perceived South Africa's distancing itself from Rhodesia as being an early move in the process that led to majority rule in South Africa itself.[\[103\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-104) > In 1976 South Africa saw settlement of the Rhodesian question as vital on several fronts: to cauterise the wound of the psychological blow … caused by her defeat in the Angolan conflict; to pre-empt possible Cuban intervention in Rhodesia and the possibility of South Africa being sucked into another [Cold War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War "Cold War") regional conflict without the support and endorsement of the western powers In the latter 1970s, the militants had successfully put the economy of Rhodesia under significant pressure while the numbers of guerrillas in the country were steadily increasing.[\[105\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-106)[\[106\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-107) The government abandoned its early strategy of trying to defend the borders in favour of trying to defend key economic areas and lines of communication with South Africa, while the rest of the countryside became a patchwork of "[no-go areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No-go_area "No-go area")". By the late 1970s, Rhodesia's front-line forces contained about 25,000 regular troops and police – backed up by relatively strong army and police reserves.[\[107\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-108) Its mechanised contingent consisted of light armoured cars and improvised [mine-protected](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MRAP "MRAP") armoured personnel carriers, complemented by eight tanks (Polish built [T-55LD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T-54/T-55_Operators_and_variants#Poland "T-54/T-55 Operators and variants") tanks), delivered in the last year of the war. The [Rhodesian Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_Air_Force "Rhodesian Air Force") operated an assortment of both [Canberra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Electric_Canberra "English Electric Canberra") light bombers, [Hawker Hunter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawker_Hunter "Hawker Hunter") fighter bombers, older [de Havilland Vampire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Havilland_Vampire "De Havilland Vampire") jets as well as a somewhat antiquated, but still potent, helicopter arm. These forces, including highly trained special operations units, were capable of launching devastating raids on resistance movement camps outside the country, as in [Operation Dingo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Dingo "Operation Dingo") in 1977 and other similar operations.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] Nevertheless, guerrilla pressure inside the country itself was steadily increasing in the latter 1970s. By 1978–1979, the war had become a contest between the guerrilla warfare placing ever increasing pressure on the Rhodesian regime and civil population, and the Rhodesian government's strategy of trying to hold off the militants until external recognition for a compromise political settlement with moderate black leaders could be secured. By this time, the need to cut a deal was apparent to most Rhodesians, but not to all. Ian Smith had dismissed his intransigent Defence Minister, [P. K. van der Byl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P._K._van_der_Byl "P. K. van der Byl"), as early as 1976.[\[108\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-109) Van der Byl was a hard-line opponent of any form of compromise with domestic opposition or the international community since before UDI. > ...it is better to fight to the last man and the last cartridge and die with some honour. Because, what is being presented to us here is a degree of humiliation... — P. K. van der Byl in 1977, commenting on a British peace plan.[\[109\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-110) Van der Byl eventually retired to his country estate outside [Cape Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Town "Cape Town"), but there were elements in Rhodesia, mainly embittered former security force personnel, who forcibly opposed majority rule up to and well beyond the establishment of majority rule.[\[110\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-111) New white immigrants continued to arrive in Rhodesia right up to the eve of majority rule.[\[111\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-112) #### Intensification of the Bush War \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rhodesia&action=edit§ion=11 "Edit section: Intensification of the Bush War")\] The work of journalists such as [Lord Richard Cecil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Richard_Cecil "Lord Richard Cecil"), son of [Robert Gascoyne-Cecil, 6th Marquess of Salisbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Gascoyne-Cecil,_6th_Marquess_of_Salisbury "Robert Gascoyne-Cecil, 6th Marquess of Salisbury"), stiffened the morale of Rhodesians and their overseas supporters.[\[112\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-113) Lord Richard produced news reports for [ITN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ITN "ITN") which typically contrasted the "incompetent" insurgents with the "superbly professional" government troops.[\[113\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-114) A group of ZANLA fighters killed Lord Richard on 20 April 1978 when he was accompanying a Rhodesian airborne unit employed in [Fire Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fire_Force_/(Rhodesia/) "Fire Force (Rhodesia)") Operations.[\[114\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-115) The shooting down on 3 September 1978 of the civilian [Air Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Rhodesia "Air Rhodesia") airliner, a [Vickers Viscount](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vickers_Viscount "Vickers Viscount") named the _[Hunyani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Rhodesia_Flight_825 "Air Rhodesia Flight 825")_, in the [Kariba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kariba,_Zimbabwe "Kariba, Zimbabwe") area by ZIPRA fighters using a [surface-to-air missile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-to-air_missile "Surface-to-air missile"), with the subsequent massacre of 10 of its 18 survivors, is widely considered to be the event that finally destroyed the Rhodesians' will to continue the war. Although militarily insignificant, the loss of this aircraft (and a second Viscount, named the _[Umniati](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Rhodesia_Flight_827 "Air Rhodesia Flight 827")_, in 1979) demonstrated the reach of resistance movements extended to Rhodesian civil society.[\[115\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-116) The Rhodesians' means to continue the war were also eroding fast. In December 1978, a ZANLA unit penetrated the outskirts of Salisbury and fired a volley of rockets and [incendiary device](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incendiary_device "Incendiary device") rounds into the main oil storage depot – the most heavily defended economic asset in the country. The storage tanks burned for five days, giving off a column of smoke that could be seen 130 kilometres (80 mi) away. Five hundred thousand barrels (79,000 m3) of petroleum product (comprising Rhodesia's strategic oil reserve) were lost.[\[116\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-117) The government's defence spending increased from R$30 million, 8.5% of the national budget in 1971 to 1972, to R$400 m in 1978 to 1979, 47% of the national budget. In 1980, the post-independence government of Zimbabwe inherited a US$500 million national debt.[\[117\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-118) [![Image 11](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2b/Internal_Settlement.jpg/250px-Internal_Settlement.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Internal_Settlement.jpg) Signing of the Rhodesian Internal Settlement (from left: Bishop Abel Muzorewa, [Ian Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Smith "Ian Smith"), [Jeremiah Chirau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremiah_Chirau "Jeremiah Chirau") and [Ndabaningi Sithole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ndabaningi_Sithole "Ndabaningi Sithole")) The Rhodesian army continued its "mobile counter-offensive" strategy of holding key positions ("vital asset ground") while carrying out raids into the no-go areas and into neighbouring countries. While often extraordinarily successful in inflicting heavy guerrilla casualties, such raids also on occasion failed to achieve their objectives. In April 1979 special forces carried out a raid on [Joshua Nkomo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Nkomo "Joshua Nkomo")'s residence in [Lusaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lusaka "Lusaka"), [Zambia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zambia "Zambia"), with the stated intention of assassinating him.[\[118\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-119) Nkomo and his family left hastily a few hours before the raid – having clearly been warned that the raid was coming. In 1979, some special forces units were accused of using counterinsurgent operations as cover for ivory poaching and smuggling. Colonel [Reid-Daly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reid-Daly "Reid-Daly") (commander of the [Selous Scouts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selous_Scouts "Selous Scouts")) discovered that his phone was bugged and after challenging a superior officer on this issue was court martialled for insubordination. He received the lightest sentence possible, a caution, but he continued to fight his conviction and eventually resigned his commission and left the Army. By 1978–1979, up to 70% of the regular army was composed of black soldiers (though both the army and police reserves remained overwhelmingly white). By 1979 there were also 30 black commissioned officers in the regular army. While there was never any suggestion of disloyalty among the soldiers from predominantly black units (in particular within the Selous Scouts or the [Rhodesian African Rifles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_African_Rifles "Rhodesian African Rifles") – RAR), some argue that, by the time of the 1980 election, many of the RAR soldiers voted for Robert Mugabe.[\[119\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-120) As the result of an [Internal Settlement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internal_Settlement "Internal Settlement") signed on 3 March 1978 between the Rhodesian government and the moderate African nationalist parties, which were not in exile and not involved in the war, elections were held in April 1979. The [United African National Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_African_National_Council "United African National Council") (UANC) party won a majority in this election, and its leader, [Abel Muzorewa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abel_Muzorewa "Abel Muzorewa") (a [United Methodist Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Methodist_Church "United Methodist Church") bishop), became the country's first black prime minister on 1 June 1979. The country's name was changed to [Zimbabwe Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_Rhodesia "Zimbabwe Rhodesia"). The internal settlement left control of the country's police, security forces, civil service and judiciary in white hands, for the moment. It assured whites of about one-third of the seats in parliament. It was essentially a power-sharing arrangement between white people and black people which, in the eyes of many, particularly the insurgents, did not amount to majority rule.[\[120\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-121) However, the [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") voted to end economic sanctions against Zimbabwe Rhodesia on 12 June.[\[121\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-endsanctions-122) While the 1979 election was described by the Rhodesian government as non-racial and democratic, it did not include the main nationalist parties ZANU and ZAPU. In spite of offers from Ian Smith, the latter parties declined to participate in an election in which their political position would be insecure and under a proposed constitution which they had played no part in drafting and which was perceived as retaining strong white minority privilege. Bishop Muzorewa's government did not receive international recognition. The Bush War continued unabated and sanctions were not lifted. The international community refused to accept the validity of any agreement which did not incorporate the main nationalist parties. The British government (then led by the recently elected [Margaret Thatcher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Thatcher "Margaret Thatcher")) issued invitations to all parties to attend a peace conference at [Lancaster House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancaster_House "Lancaster House"). These negotiations took place in London in late 1979. The three-month-long conference almost failed to reach conclusion, due to disagreements on [land reform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_reform_in_Zimbabwe "Land reform in Zimbabwe"), but resulted in the [Lancaster House Agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancaster_House_Agreement "Lancaster House Agreement"). UDI ended, and Rhodesia temporarily reverted to the status of a British colony (the 'Colony of Southern Rhodesia').[\[122\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-123) As per the agreement, [Lord Soames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Soames "Christopher Soames") became governor with full legislative and executive powers. The Lancaster House Agreement further provided for a ceasefire which was followed by an internationally supervised general election, held in [February 1980](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesian_general_election,_1980 "Southern Rhodesian general election, 1980"). ZANU led by [Robert Mugabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe "Robert Mugabe") won this election, some alleged,\[_[who?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Words_to_watch#Unsupported_attributions "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch")_\] by terrorising its political opposition, including supporters of ZAPU, through former insurgents that had not confined themselves to the designated guerrilla assembly points, as stipulated by the Lancaster House Agreement. The observers and Soames were accused of looking the other way, and Mugabe's victory was certified. Nevertheless, few could doubt that Mugabe's support within his majority Shona tribal group was extremely strong. The Rhodesian military seriously considered mounting a coup against a perceived stolen election ("[Operation Quartz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Quartz "Operation Quartz")") to prevent ZANU from taking over the country.[\[123\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-124) The alleged coup was to include the assassination of Mugabe and coordinated assaults on guerrilla assembly points throughout the country. The plan was eventually scuttled, as it was obvious that Mugabe enjoyed widespread support from the black majority despite voter intimidation, as well as the fact that the coup would gain no external support, and a conflagration which would engulf the country was seen as inevitable. ### Republic of Zimbabwe (1980) \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rhodesia&action=edit§ion=13 "Edit section: Republic of Zimbabwe (1980)")\] On 18 April 1980, the country became independent within the [Commonwealth of Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_Nations "Commonwealth of Nations") as the Republic of Zimbabwe, and its capital, Salisbury, was renamed [Harare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harare "Harare") two years later. Rhodesia is equivalent in territory to modern [Zimbabwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe "Zimbabwe"). It was a [landlocked country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landlocked_country "Landlocked country") in [southern Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Africa "Southern Africa"), lying between latitudes [15°](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/15th_parallel_south "15th parallel south") and [23°S](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/23rd_parallel_south "23rd parallel south"), and longitudes [25°](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/25th_meridian_east "25th meridian east") and [34°E](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/34th_meridian_east "34th meridian east"). It was bordered by [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa") to the south, the [Bechuanaland Protectorate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bechuanaland_Protectorate "Bechuanaland Protectorate") (later [Botswana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Botswana "Botswana")) to the west and southwest, [Zambia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zambia "Zambia") to the northwest, and [Mozambique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mozambique "Mozambique") to the east and northeast. Its northwest corner was roughly 150 metres (500 feet) from [South West Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_West_Africa "South West Africa") (present-day [Namibia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Namibia "Namibia")), South Africa, nearly forming a four-nation [quadripoint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadripoint "Quadripoint"). Most of the country was elevated, consisting of a central plateau (high veld) stretching from the southwest northwards with altitudes between 1,000 and 1,600 m (3,300 and 5,200 ft). The country's extreme east was mountainous, this area being known as the [Eastern Highlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Highlands "Eastern Highlands"), with [Mount Inyangani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Nyangani "Mount Nyangani") as the highest point at 2,592 m (8,504 ft).\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] Rhodesia had a [tropical climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_climate "Tropical climate") with many local variations. The southern areas were known for their heat and aridity, parts of the central plateau received frost in winter, the [Zambezi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zambezi "Zambezi") valley was also known for its extreme heat and the Eastern Highlands usually experienced cool temperatures and the highest rainfall in the country. The country's rainy season was from late October to March and the hot climate was moderated by increasing altitude. The country was faced with recurring droughts, and severe storms were rare.[\[124\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Baughan,_M._2005-125) The country was mostly savannah, although the moist and mountainous eastern highlands supported areas of tropical evergreen and hardwood forests. Trees found in these Eastern Highlands included [teak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teak "Teak"), [mahogany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahogany "Mahogany"), enormous specimens of [strangling fig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strangler_fig "Strangler fig"), [forest newtonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newtonia_buchananii "Newtonia buchananii"), big leaf, [white stinkwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celtis_africana "Celtis africana"), [chirinda stinkwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celtis_mildbraedii "Celtis mildbraedii"), [knobthorn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senegalia_nigrescens "Senegalia nigrescens") and many others. In the low-lying parts of the country, [fever trees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vachellia_xanthophloea "Vachellia xanthophloea"), [mopane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mopane "Mopane"), [combretum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combretum "Combretum") and [baobabs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adansonia "Adansonia") abound. Much of the country was covered by [miombo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miombo "Miombo") woodland, dominated by [brachystegia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brachystegia "Brachystegia") species and others. Among the numerous flowers and shrubs were [hibiscus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hibiscus "Hibiscus"), [flame lily](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flame_lily "Flame lily"), [snake lily](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scadoxus_puniceus "Scadoxus puniceus"), [spider lily](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spider_lily "Spider lily"), [leonotus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonotis "Leonotis"), [cassia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassia_/(genus/) "Cassia (genus)"), [tree wisteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisteria "Wisteria") and [dombeya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dombeya "Dombeya"). There were around 350 species of mammals that can be found in Rhodesia. There were also many snakes and lizards, over 500 bird species, and 131 fish species. Government and politics ----------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rhodesia&action=edit§ion=17 "Edit section: Government and politics")\] [![Image 12](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a3/Flag_of_the_President_of_Rhodesia_%281970%E2%80%931979%29.svg/330px-Flag_of_the_President_of_Rhodesia_%281970%E2%80%931979%29.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Flag_of_the_President_of_Rhodesia_/(1970%E2%80%931979/).svg) The presidential flag of Rhodesia Although Southern Rhodesia never gained full [Dominion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominion "Dominion") status within the [Commonwealth of Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_Nations "Commonwealth of Nations"), Southern Rhodesians ruled themselves from the attainment of '[Responsible Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Responsible_government "Responsible government")' in 1923. Its electoral register had property and education qualifications. Over the years various electoral arrangements made at a national and municipal level upheld these standards. For example, the franchise for the first [Southern Rhodesian Legislative Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesian_Legislative_Council "Southern Rhodesian Legislative Council") election in 1899 contained the following requirement: > voters to be British subjects, male, 21 years of age and older, able to write their address and occupation, and then to fulfil the following financial requirements: (a) ownership of a registered mining claim in Southern Rhodesia, or (b) occupying immovable property worth £75, or (c) receiving wages or salary of £50 per annum in Southern Rhodesia. Six months' continuous residence was also required for qualifications (b) and (c). Following [Cecil Rhodes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Rhodes "Cecil Rhodes")'s dictum of "equal rights for all civilised men", there was an implicit, albeit not an overt, racial component to the franchise, which effectively excluded a majority of native black people from the electorate via such means as [property qualifications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Property_qualification "Property qualification").[\[125\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-126) Up until the 1950s, Southern Rhodesia had a vibrant political life with right and left wing parties competing for power. The [Rhodesian Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_Labour_Party "Rhodesian Labour Party") held seats in the Assembly and in municipal councils throughout the 1920s and 1930s. From 1953 to 1958, the prime minister was [Garfield Todd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garfield_Todd "Garfield Todd"), a liberal who did much to promote the development of the black community through investment in education, housing and healthcare. However, the government forced Todd from office because his proposed reforms were seen by many whites as too radical. From 1958 onwards, white settler politics consolidated and ossified around resistance to majority rule, setting the stage for UDI. The 1961 Constitution governed Southern Rhodesia and independent Rhodesia up until 1969, using the Westminster Parliamentary System modified by a system of separate voter rolls with differing property and education qualifications, without regard to race. Whites ended up with the majority of Assembly seats with Whites attaining 50 out of 66 seats. Blacks would only attain 16 out of the 66 seats in the Rhodesian Parliament. The 1969 republican constitution established a [bicameral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicameral "Bicameral") Parliament consisting of an indirectly elected [Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_of_Rhodesia "Senate of Rhodesia") and a directly elected [House of Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Assembly_of_Rhodesia "House of Assembly of Rhodesia"), effectively reserving the majority of seats for whites. The office of [president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Rhodesia "President of Rhodesia") had only ceremonial significance with the prime minister holding executive power. The Constitution of the short-lived [Zimbabwe Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_Rhodesia "Zimbabwe Rhodesia"), which saw a black-led government elected for the first time, reserved 28 of the 100 parliamentary seats for whites. The independence constitution agreed at [Lancaster House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancaster_House_Agreement "Lancaster House Agreement") watered those provisions down and reserved 20 out of 100 seats for whites in the House of Assembly and 8 out of 40 seats in the Senate. The constitution prohibited Zimbabwe authorities from altering the Constitution for seven years without unanimous consent and required a three-quarters vote in Parliament for a further three years. The government amended the Constitution in 1987 to abolish the seats reserved for whites, and replace the office of [prime minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Zimbabwe "Prime Minister of Zimbabwe") with an executive president. In 1990, the government abolished the Senate. ### Administrative divisions \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rhodesia&action=edit§ion=18 "Edit section: Administrative divisions")\] [![Image 13](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/90/Rhodesia_adm_location_map_with_names.svg/500px-Rhodesia_adm_location_map_with_names.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rhodesia_adm_location_map_with_names.svg) [Administrative divisions of Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Provinces_of_Rhodesia&action=edit&redlink=1 "Provinces of Rhodesia (page does not exist)") Rhodesia had a [centralised government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centralised_government "Centralised government") and was divided into seven provinces and two cities with provincial status, for administrative purposes. security forces, as well as British fears of a direct South African intervention on behalf of the rogue colony, preempted the further consideration of military options.[\[126\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Good-127) For much of its existence, Rhodesia maintained a small professional standing army of 3,400 troops, about a third of whom were black volunteers.[\[126\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Good-127) In the tradition of many colonial armies, it was primarily organised into light infantry battalions trained and equipped for counter-insurgency warfare or internal security actions,[\[127\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Arnold-128) and possessed little artillery or armour.[\[126\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Good-127) The [Royal Rhodesian Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Rhodesian_Air_Force "Royal Rhodesian Air Force") (RRAF) had 1,000 personnel and six squadrons of aircraft, including forty to fifty [Hawker Hunter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawker_Hunter "Hawker Hunter") and [de Havilland Vampire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Havilland_Vampire "De Havilland Vampire") strike aircraft and [English Electric Canberra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Electric_Canberra "English Electric Canberra") light bombers.[\[126\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Good-127) It also possessed a helicopter squadron, a transport squadron, and a light reconnaissance squadron.[\[126\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Good-127) The Rhodesian military was backed by the [British South Africa Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_South_Africa_Police "British South Africa Police") (BSAP), a well-equipped police force whose title was derived from the law enforcement division of the British South Africa Company.[\[126\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Good-127) The BSAP had armoured vehicles of its own and a potent paramilitary capability.[\[126\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Good-127) Domestic and external intelligence gathering were vested in the [Central Intelligence Organisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Intelligence_Organisation "Central Intelligence Organisation") (CIO).[\[128\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-COIN-129) As a result of the escalating rural insurgency, the Rhodesian Security Forces began to depend more heavily on white conscripts and reservists of the Territorial Force and Territorial reserves.[\[127\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Arnold-128) Regular units remained small throughout the Rhodesian Bush War but became increasingly specialised and were often able to have an effect utterly disproportionate to their size.[\[129\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-mcnab2002-130) The security forces included a disproportionate number of personnel who had seen action during the [First Malayan Emergency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Malayan_Emergency "First Malayan Emergency") as well as the [Aden Emergency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency "Aden Emergency"), and their experience gave Rhodesia's defence establishment a solid grounding in counter-insurgency warfare and small unit tactics in particular.[\[128\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-COIN-129) Nevertheless, the vastness of the operational area and Rhodesia's limited manpower pool left the army, air force, and BSAP constantly overstretched.[\[128\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-COIN-129) Budgetary and resource restraints, coupled with manpower shortages, meant the security forces could not expand quickly enough to match the guerrilla movements, and were almost always outnumbered.[\[128\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-COIN-129) Rhodesian units compensated for their disadvantage in this regard by pursuing an aggressive preemptive and counterstrike strategy, raiding neighbouring states to destroy guerrilla forces in their external sanctuaries.[\[128\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-COIN-129) All white, male residents aged eighteen to twenty-three were obligated to fulfill four and a half months (later extended to nine months) of full-time [national service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_service "National service").[\[126\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Good-127) This was followed by a three-year reservist obligation.[\[126\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Good-127) By 1974, the national service intakes had been doubled, and white men over twenty-three were also conscripted.[\[127\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Arnold-128) In 1978, the Rhodesian Army had about 14,000 white national servicemen, but continued manpower shortages forced it to recruit black volunteers in larger numbers and extend compulsory military service to all white males up to sixty years of age.[\[127\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Arnold-128) By the end of the Rhodesian Bush War virtually all male white residents were either serving in the military or police in a full-time or part-time capacity.[\[127\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Arnold-128) The size of the Rhodesian Army had swelled to about 20,000 personnel, and the BSAP to over 40,000, including reservists.[\[127\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Arnold-128) ### Biological and chemical warfare \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rhodesia&action=edit§ion=20 "Edit section: Biological and chemical warfare")\] From 1975 to 1980, the Rhodesian government made several attempts to weaponise chemical and biological agents.[\[130\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Glenn_Cross_1980-131) Members of the security forces contaminated supplies before replacing them in guerrilla caches or planted them in rural stores to be stolen by the guerrillas during raids.[\[131\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-132) They also poisoned water sources along known infiltration routes along the Rhodesian border, forcing their opponents to travel through more arid regions or carry more water during their treks.[\[132\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-133) The chemical agents most used in the Rhodesian chemical and biological warfare (CBW) programme were [parathion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parathion "Parathion") (an organophosphate insecticide) and [thallium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thallium "Thallium") (a heavy metal commonly found in rodenticide).[\[133\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-134) The weapons the Rhodesians selected for use also included _Vibrio cholerae_ (causative agent of [cholera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cholera "Cholera")) and possibly _Bacillus anthracis_ (causative agent of [anthrax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthrax "Anthrax")). They also looked at using _Rickettsia prowazekii_ (causative agent of epidemic [typhus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Typhus "Typhus")), and _Salmonella typhi_ (causative agent of [typhoid fever](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Typhoid_fever "Typhoid fever")), and toxins such as [ricin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricin "Ricin") and [botulinum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Botulinum "Botulinum") toxin.[\[130\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Glenn_Cross_1980-131) Biological agents, namely _Vibrio cholerae_, had some impact on the fighting capability of ZANLA.[\[134\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-the_plague_wars-135) Some former officers of the Rhodesian Security Forces alleged that anthrax was used covertly during the late 1970s, but this has been disputed.[\[130\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Glenn_Cross_1980-131) Use of _anthracis_, ricin, or botulinum toxin was favoured during assassination attempts of prominent guerrilla commanders.[\[130\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Glenn_Cross_1980-131) Economically, [Southern Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia "Southern Rhodesia") developed an economy that was narrowly based on the production of a few [primary products](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primary_products "Primary products"), notably, [chromium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium "Chromium") and [tobacco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tobacco "Tobacco"). It was therefore vulnerable to the economic cycle. The deep [recession of the 1930s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Great_Depression "The Great Depression") gave way to a post-war boom. This boom prompted the immigration of about 200,000 whites between 1945 and 1970, taking the white population up to 307,000. A large number of these immigrants were of British working-class origin, with others coming from the [Belgian Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgian_Congo "Belgian Congo"), [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Kenya "British Kenya"), [Tanzania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanzania "Tanzania"), and later [Angola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Angola "Portuguese Angola") and [Mozambique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Mozambique "Portuguese Mozambique"). They established a relatively balanced economy, transforming what was once a primary producer dependent on backwoods farming into an modest industrial power which spawned a strong manufacturing sector, [iron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron "Iron") and [steel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steel "Steel") industries, and modern mining ventures. These economic successes owed a lot to the immigration of skilled labour and backing from South Africa. The economy of the state of Rhodesia sustained international sanctions for a decade following the declaration of its independence, a resistance which waned as more southern African states declared independence and majority rule as well as the destruction caused by the [Rhodesian Bush War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_Bush_War "Rhodesian Bush War"). A central feature of the white community in Rhodesia was its transience, as white settlers were just as likely to leave Rhodesia after a few years as permanently settle; for example, of the 700 Britons who were the first white settlers, arriving in 1890, only 15 were still living in Rhodesia in 1924.[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Brownell-102): 6593  As the white population of Rhodesia had a low birth rate (18 per 1,000 compared to the African rate of 48 per 1,000[\[135\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Paxton-136)), maintaining white population growth was largely dependent upon taking in new white immigrants with immigration accounting for 60% of the growth of the white Rhodesian population between 1955 and 1972.[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Brownell-102) In the ten years after the nation's declaration of independence from Britain, around 70,000 from the white population of Rhodesia emigrated from the nation. 45% of the emigration was to South Africa, as it was geographically adjacent and shared similarities in climate, topography, economic standards, and social customs. The remaining 55% chiefly headed to other mainly white, English-speaking nations at the time: the United Kingdom, Australia, Canada, and New Zealand.[\[136\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-137) However, the American historian Josiah Brownell noted that the turnover rate for white residents in Rhodesia was very high, as Rhodesia took in a total of 255,692 white immigrants between 1955 and 1979 while the same period a total of 246,583 whites emigrated. Even during the boom years of the late 1950s, when Rhodesia took in an average of 13,666 white immigrants per year, mostly from the United Kingdom and South Africa, an average of about 7,666 whites emigrated annually. Between 1961 and 1965, Rhodesia took in an average of 8,225 white immigrants per year while also having an average white emigration of 12,912 per year. Many prospective white immigrants in Rhodesia arrived seeking economic opportunities and departed with fluctuations in the security situation as the Bush War intensified. A substantial number were uninterested in settling there permanently and did not apply for Rhodesian citizenship, despite a much-publicised 1967 campaign urging them to do so.[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Brownell-102) Brownell asserted that patriotism in the white community was "shallow" due to its essentially expatriate character. He also claimed that the majority of white immigrants in the late 1960s and early 1970s were unskilled laborers who competed with the country's black African workforce and did not contribute badly needed technical or professional skills to the country, arguing that this was due to government policy aimed at making white immigration as "unselective as possible" and guaranteeing every white immigrant a job. The population of Rhodesia boomed during the late 1960s due to immigration and an exceptional rate of natural increase among its black citizens, the highest in sub-Saharan Africa at the time.[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Brownell-102)

White Rhodesians mostly spoke English, with a minority that spoke [Afrikaans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afrikaans "Afrikaans"). Approximately 70% of black Rhodesians spoke [Shona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shona_language "Shona language"), and around 20% spoke [Ndebele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ndebele_language "Northern Ndebele language").[\[138\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-139) A majority of [Rhodesia's Indian community](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indians_in_Zimbabwe "Indians in Zimbabwe") spoke [Gujarati](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gujarati_language "Gujarati language") and a minority spoke [Hindi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindi "Hindi"). Rhodesia predominantly adhered to [Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity "Christianity"), with [Protestantism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestantism "Protestantism") being the largest denomination. However, many native Africans still adhered to [traditional African religions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traditional_African_religions "Traditional African religions"). Throughout the period of its [Unilateral Declaration of Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence_/(Rhodesia/) "Unilateral Declaration of Independence (Rhodesia)") (1965 to 1979), Rhodesia pursued a foreign policy of attempting to secure recognition as an independent country, and insisting that its political system would include 'gradual steps to majority rule.' Ardently anti-communist, Rhodesia tried to present itself to the West as a front-line state against communist expansion in Africa, to little avail. Rhodesia received little international recognition during its existence; recognition only occurred after elections in 1980 and a transition to majority rule. Rhodesia wished to retain its economic prosperity and also feared communist elements in the rebel forces, and thus felt their policy of a gradual progression to black majority rule was justified. However, the international community refused to accept this rationale, believing that their policies were perpetuating racism. This attitude was part of the larger [decolonisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decolonisation "Decolonisation") context, during which Western powers such as the United Kingdom, France, and Belgium hastened to grant independence to their colonies in Africa. Rhodesia was originally a [British colony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_colony "British colony"). Although [decolonisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decolonisation "Decolonisation") in Africa had begun after World War II, it began accelerating in the early 1960s, causing Britain to negotiate independence rapidly with several of its colonies. During this period, it adopted a foreign policy called [NIBMAR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NIBMAR "NIBMAR"), or No Independence Before Majority African Rule, mandating democratic reforms that placed governance in the hands of the majority black Africans. The governing white minority of Rhodesia, led by Ian Smith, opposed the policy and its implications. On 11 November 1965, Rhodesia's minority white government made a [unilateral declaration of independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence "Rhodesia's Unilateral Declaration of Independence") (UDI) from the United Kingdom, as it became apparent that negotiations would not lead to independence under the white regime. The United Kingdom government immediately brought in legislation ([Southern Rhodesia Act 1965](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_Act_1965 "Southern Rhodesia Act 1965")) which formally abolished all Rhodesian government institutions. This move made life difficult for Rhodesian citizens who wished to travel internationally as passports issued by Rhodesia's UDI administration were not recognised as valid;[\[139\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Passports_invalidated-140) in January 1966, the British issued a statement accepting as valid any passport issued before the declaration of independence and allowing six-month United Kingdom passports to be granted when they expired – provided that the bearer declared they did not intend to aid the UDI Rhodesian government.[\[140\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-1966_statement-141) Developments in Britain helped to alienate the white Rhodesian population from the former mother country, namely Queen [Elizabeth II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_II "Elizabeth II")'s 1966 speech to the [Parliament of Jamaica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_Jamaica "Parliament of Jamaica") where she endorsed majority rule and her attempt in 1968 to block the hanging of what Rhodesians perceived as Zimbabwean nationalist terrorists.[\[141\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-142) Until late 1969, Rhodesia still recognised Queen Elizabeth II as head of state, even though it opposed the British government itself for hindering its goals of independence. However she refused to accept the title _Queen of Rhodesia_ and eventually the Smith government abandoned their attempts to remain loyal to the British Crown. In a 1969 referendum, a majority of the electorate voted to declare Rhodesia an independent republic. The hope being that this move would facilitate recognition as an independent state by the international community, but the issue of white minority rule remained and continued to hinder this effort, and like the UDI before it, the proclamation of a republic lacked international recognition. The British public overall viewed the issue of Rhodesia and UDI as a distant and anachronistic one that they cared relatively little about and saw any expedient response to it by their government as satisfactory. Most Britons saw the end of Rhodesia's [white supremacist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_supremacy "White supremacy") [timocracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timocracy "Timocracy") as inevitable and justified. Although the majority Britons opposed military intervention against the renegade Rhodesian state, this opinion was not uniformly held.[\[142\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-143) After the declaration of independence, and indeed for the entire duration of its existence, Rhodesia did not receive official recognition from any state, although it did maintain diplomatic relations with South Africa, which was then under [apartheid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apartheid "Apartheid"). South Africa did not recognise Rhodesia to preserve its fragile positions with other nations, but frequently assisted the Rhodesian state. [Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estado_Novo_/(Portugal/) "Estado Novo (Portugal)") maintained informal relations until the [Carnation Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnation_Revolution "Carnation Revolution") of 1974. The day following the declaration of independence, the [United Nations Security Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council "United Nations Security Council") passed a resolution ([S/RES/216](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council_Resolution_216 "United Nations Security Council Resolution 216")) calling upon all states not to accord Rhodesia recognition, and to refrain from any assistance. The Security Council also imposed selective mandatory economic sanctions, which were later made comprehensive. The US, despite voting in favour of the sanctions at the UNSC, violated them to buy chromium ore from Rhodesia.[\[143\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-144) Kenneth Kaunda, president of Zambia, also accused western oil companies of violating the sanctions and selling oil to Rhodesia.[\[144\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-145) ### International perspective \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rhodesia&action=edit§ion=29 "Edit section: International perspective")\] Rhodesia's Unilateral Declaration of Independence from the United Kingdom on 11 November 1965 was promptly condemned by the international community. The United Nations Security Council Resolution 216 of 12 November 1965 called "upon all States not to recognise this illegal racist minority regime in Southern Rhodesia."[\[145\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-146) Rhodesia campaigned for international acceptance and invoked the doctrine of [non-intervention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-intervention "Non-intervention") in internal affairs as justification for rebuking external criticism of its internal policies. However, the emerging doctrine of [self-determination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-determination "Self-determination") in colonial situations meant that most nations regarded Rhodesia's self-declared independence as illegitimate. Zambia, formerly [Northern Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Rhodesia "Northern Rhodesia"), took a pragmatic approach towards Rhodesia. [Kenneth Kaunda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Kaunda "Kenneth Kaunda"), heavily dependent on access through Rhodesia for his nation's copper ore exports, fuel, and power imports unofficially worked with the Rhodesian government. Rhodesia still allowed Zambia to export and import its goods through its territory to Mozambique ports, despite the Zambian government's official policy of hostility and non-recognition of the post-UDI Smith Administration. The United States, like all other Western nations, refused to recognise Rhodesia, but unlike others allowed its [Consulate-General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consulate-General "Consulate-General") to function as a communications conduit between the US government in Washington, DC and the Rhodesian government in Salisbury. When Rhodesia set up the [Rhodesian Information Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rhodesian_Information_Office&action=edit&redlink=1 "Rhodesian Information Office (page does not exist)") in Washington, DC, [OAS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organization_of_American_States "Organization of American States") nations loudly protested. The US government responded by saying the Rhodesian mission and its staff had no official diplomatic status and violated no US laws. Portugal pursued a middle path with Rhodesia. While not officially recognising Rhodesia under Ian Smith, the government of [António Salazar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ant%C3%B3nio_Salazar "António Salazar") did permit Rhodesia to establish a [representative mission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_mission_in_Lisbon "Rhodesian mission in Lisbon") in Lisbon, and permitted Rhodesian exports and imports through their colony of Mozambique. The Portuguese government in power at that time, authoritarian and ardently anti-communist, gave active behind-the-scenes support in Rhodesia's fight against the guerrilla groups. South Africa, itself under international pressure as a white minority government, pursued a policy of [détente](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C3%A9tente "Détente") with the black African states at the time. These states wanted South Africa to pressure Ian Smith to accept a faster transition to majority rule in Rhodesia, in return for pledges of non-interference in South Africa's internal affairs. Prime Minister [John Vorster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Vorster "John Vorster"), believing majority rule in Rhodesia would lead to international acceptance for South Africa, used a number of tactics to pressure Smith. The South African government held up shipments of fuel and ammunition and pulled out friendly South African forces from Rhodesia. The combined loss of Mozambique and the loss of support from South Africa dealt critical blows to the Rhodesian government. ### Diplomatic relations \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rhodesia&action=edit§ion=30 "Edit section: Diplomatic relations")\] After the UDI, Rhodesia maintained several overseas missions, including [Pretoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pretoria "Pretoria"),[\[146\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-147) and until 1975, [Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon "Lisbon") in Portugal and Lourenço Marques (now [Maputo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maputo "Maputo")) in [Mozambique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mozambique "Mozambique").[\[147\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-148) Since 1961, Rhodesia had an "Accredited Diplomatic Representative" with [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa"), heading a "Rhodesian Diplomatic Mission" or [_de facto_ embassy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_facto_embassy "De facto embassy").[\[148\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-149) Before South Africa left the [Commonwealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_Nations "Commonwealth of Nations") that year, the then [Southern Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia "Southern Rhodesia") had exchanged High Commissioners with the then [Union of South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_of_South_Africa "Union of South Africa"), but following the change in status, the Republic now had a "South African Diplomatic Mission" in [Salisbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harare "Harare").[\[149\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-lloyd-150) During 1965, the government of Rhodesia made moves to establish a [mission in Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_mission_in_Lisbon "Rhodesian mission in Lisbon") separate from the British Embassy, with its own accredited representative, having previously been able to establish its own consulate in Lourenço Marques, capital of [Portuguese Mozambique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Mozambique "Portuguese Mozambique").[\[150\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-151) This prompted protests from the British government, which was determined that the representative, Harry Reedman, should be a nominal member of the British Ambassador's staff.[\[151\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-152) For their part, the Portuguese authorities sought a compromise whereby they would accept Reedman as an independent representative but deny him diplomatic status.[\[152\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-153) The Rhodesian Information Office in [Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.") remained open following UDI, but its director, [Ken Towsey](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ken_Towsey&action=edit&redlink=1 "Ken Towsey (page does not exist)"), and his staff were deprived of their diplomatic status.[\[153\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-154) Previously, there had been a "Minister for Rhodesian Affairs" operating under the aegis of the [British Embassy in Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Embassy_in_Washington "British Embassy in Washington"),[\[154\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-155) as well representatives in [Tokyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo "Tokyo") and [Bonn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bonn "Bonn").[\[155\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-156) Following the country's independence as [Zimbabwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe "Zimbabwe"), Towsey became chargé d'affaires at the new embassy.[\[156\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-157) The High Commission in London, known as [Rhodesia House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia_House "Rhodesia House"), continued to function until it was closed in 1969 following the decision by white Rhodesians in a [referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_constitutional_referendum,_1969 "Rhodesian constitutional referendum, 1969") to make the country a republic, along with the "British Residual Mission" in [Salisbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harare "Harare").[\[157\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-158) Prior to its closure, the mission flew the newly adopted [Flag of Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flag_of_Rhodesia "Flag of Rhodesia"), considered illegal by the [Foreign Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_and_Commonwealth_Office "Foreign and Commonwealth Office"), prompting calls by [Labour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_/(UK/) "Labour Party (UK)") MP [Willie Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Hamilton "Willie Hamilton") for its removal.[\[158\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-159) In Australia, the federal government sought to close the [Rhodesia Information Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia_Information_Centre "Rhodesia Information Centre") in [Sydney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney "Sydney"),[\[159\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-160) but it remained open, operating under the jurisdiction of the state of [New South Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_South_Wales "New South Wales").[\[160\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-161) In 1973, the [Labor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Labor_Party "Australian Labor Party") government of [Gough Whitlam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gough_Whitlam "Gough Whitlam") cut post and telephone links to the centre, but this was [ruled illegal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bradley_v_Commonwealth "Bradley v Commonwealth") by the [High Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Court_of_Australia "High Court of Australia").[\[161\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-162) An office was also established in [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris"), but this was closed down by the [French government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_government "French government") in 1977.[\[162\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-163) Similarly, the United States recalled its consul-general from Salisbury, and reduced consular staff,[\[163\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-164) but did not move to close its consulate until the declaration of a republic in 1970.[\[164\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-165) South Africa, however, retained its "Accredited Diplomatic Representative" after UDI,[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-google13-61) which allowed it to continue to recognise British sovereignty as well as to deal with the _de facto_ authority of the government of [Ian Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Smith "Ian Smith").[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-google257-62) The South African Diplomatic Mission in Salisbury became the only such mission remaining in the country after 1975,[\[165\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-166) when Portugal downgraded its mission to consul level,[\[166\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-167) having recalled its consul-general in Salisbury in May 1970.[\[167\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-168) After Zimbabwe's independence, the new government closed its missions in [Pretoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pretoria "Pretoria") and [Cape Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Town "Cape Town"), only maintaining a trade mission in [Johannesburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannesburg "Johannesburg"),[\[168\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-169) while the South African Diplomatic Mission in Salisbury was also closed.[\[169\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-170) The growing intensity of the civil war and a lack of international support eventually led the Rhodesian government to submit to an agreement with the UK in 1979. This led to internationally supervised elections, won by [Zimbabwe African National Union – Patriotic Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_African_National_Union_%E2%80%93_Patriotic_Front "Zimbabwe African National Union – Patriotic Front") and Robert Mugabe, establishing the internationally recognised [Zimbabwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe "Zimbabwe"). The most influential newspapers in the country were the _[Rhodesia Herald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia_Herald "Rhodesia Herald")_ in [Salisbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harare "Harare") and _[The Chronicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Chronicle_/(Zimbabwe/) "The Chronicle (Zimbabwe)")_ in [Bulawayo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulawayo "Bulawayo"). Following UDI, in 1976, the state-run [Rhodesian Broadcasting Corporation (RBC)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_Broadcasting_Corporation "Zimbabwe Broadcasting Corporation") took over the privately owned [Rhodesia Television (RTV)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia_Television "Rhodesia Television") service, in which it had previously acquired a 51 percent stake.[\[170\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-171) Among the news magazines published in Rhodesia under UDI were the _[Illustrated Life Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illustrated_Life_Rhodesia "Illustrated Life Rhodesia")_, while _The Valiant Years_ by Beryl Salt told the history of Rhodesia from 1890 to 1978 entirely through the medium of facsimile reproduction of articles and headlines from Rhodesian newspapers.[\[171\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-172) As Rhodesia was a former colony of the United Kingdom, all of the sports that were born in the United Kingdom enjoyed considerable popularity in Rhodesia; especially [cricket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cricket "Cricket"), [rugby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_football "Rugby football"), [water polo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_polo "Water polo"), [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football"), [netball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netball "Netball"), [golf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golf "Golf"), [tennis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennis "Tennis") (including the [Rhodesian Open Tennis Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_Open_Tennis_Championships "Rhodesian Open Tennis Championships")), [lawn bowls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawn_bowls "Lawn bowls"), [field hockey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_hockey "Field hockey"), etc. Just like neighbouring South Africa, Rhodesia was barred from both competing against and participating with [Commonwealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_Nations "Commonwealth of Nations") member countries.[\[172\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-173) One of the biggest triumphs in Rhodesia sports history was when the team defeated the New Zealand national rugby team 10-8 while the All Blacks were touring South Africa. They are 1 of 8 nations to ever defeat the All Blacks and the only non-test nation to have ever beaten them. As this was the only game the two nations ever played they also have the unique honour of having a 100% win record against the All Blacks.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] In the ten years after transforming into [Zimbabwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe "Zimbabwe"), around 60% of the white population emigrated, most to [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa") and to other mainly white, English-speaking countries where they formed immigrant communities. Politically within Zimbabwe, the consolidation of power by [Robert Mugabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe "Robert Mugabe") continued through the 1980s. Following amendments to the country's [constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Zimbabwe "Constitution of Zimbabwe") in 1987, parliamentary seats reserved for whites were abolished, and an executive presidency was created, held by [Mugabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugabe "Mugabe"). Many\[_[who?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Words_to_watch#Unsupported_attributions "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch")_\] immigrants and some of the whites who stayed in Zimbabwe became deeply nostalgic for Rhodesia. These individuals are known as "[Rhodies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodie "Rhodie")".
