17.content:
[The beliefs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jehovah%27s_Witnesses_beliefs "Jehovah's Witnesses beliefs") and [practices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jehovah%27s_Witnesses_practices "Jehovah's Witnesses practices") of [Jehovah's Witnesses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jehovah%27s_Witnesses "Jehovah's Witnesses") have [engendered controversy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Criticism_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses "Criticism of Jehovah's Witnesses") throughout [their history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses "History of Jehovah's Witnesses"). Consequently, the denomination has been opposed by local governments, communities, and religious groups. Many [Christian denominations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_denomination "Christian denomination") consider the interpretations and doctrines of Jehovah's Witnesses [heretical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heresy "Heresy"), and some professors of [religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religion "Religion") have classified the denomination as a [cult](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cult "Cult").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-1)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-2)

According to [law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law "Law") professor [Archibald Cox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archibald_Cox "Archibald Cox"), Jehovah's Witnesses in the United States were "the principal victims of [religious persecution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religious_discrimination_in_the_United_States "Religious discrimination in the United States") … they began to attract attention and provoke repression in the 1930s, when their proselytizing and numbers rapidly increased."[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-3) At times, political and religious animosity against Jehovah's Witnesses has led to [mob action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mob_action "Mob action") and [governmental](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government "Government") repression in various countries including the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses_in_the_United_States "Persecution of Jehovah's Witnesses in the United States"), [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses_in_Canada "Persecution of Jehovah's Witnesses in Canada") and [Nazi Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses_in_Nazi_Germany "Persecution of Jehovah's Witnesses in Nazi Germany").

During [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), Jehovah's Witnesses were targeted in the United States, Canada, and many other countries because they refused to serve in the military or contribute to the war effort due to their [doctrine of political neutrality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jehovah%27s_Witnesses_and_governments "Jehovah's Witnesses and governments"). In Canada, Jehovah's Witnesses were interned in camps[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-canww2-4) along with political dissidents and [people of Japanese descent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internment_of_Japanese_Canadians "Internment of Japanese Canadians").

Jehovah's Witness members have been imprisoned in many countries for their refusal of [conscription](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conscription "Conscription") or compulsory [military service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_service "Military service"). Their religious activities are banned or restricted in some countries, including [Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singapore "Singapore"), [North Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Korea "North Korea"), [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China"), [Vietnam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam "Vietnam"), [Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia") and many [Muslim-majority countries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim_world "Muslim world").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-5)

[![Image 1](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/73/Ban_on_Activities_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses.svg/250px-Ban_on_Activities_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ban_on_Activities_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses.svg)

Countries where Jehovah's Witnesses' activities are banned

In 1930, the Watch Tower Society had controlling interests in several radio stations in Australia, including [5KA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5KA "5KA"), where presenters were told to preach and in 1931 began broadcasting sermons of [Joseph Franklin Rutherford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Franklin_Rutherford "Joseph Franklin Rutherford"). In 1933, the Australian government banned Rutherford's sermons, which included diatribes against the Catholic Church and other Christian denominations, the British Empire, and the United States.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-Griffen-6) On 8 January 1941, the Watch Tower Society's stations were permanently closed down, being described as dangerous to national security. Jehovah's Witnesses was declared an illegal organization on 17 January 1941, with World War II described as "an ideal opportunity to get rid of licensees long regarded as deviant".[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-Griffen-6)

In the period between 1978 and 2004, Jehovah's Witnesses sought registration as a religious society under the 1874 law, which they were repeatedly prevented from doing by state institutions for various reasons. The [ECHR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Convention_on_Human_Rights "European Convention on Human Rights") ruled in 2008 that Austria had thus violated Articles 9, 14, 6 and 13 of the Convention on Human Rights.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-7)

During the first presidency of [Mathieu Kérékou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathieu_K%C3%A9r%C3%A9kou "Mathieu Kérékou"), activities of Jehovah's Witnesses were banned and members were forced to undergo "demystification training".[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-8)\[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_\]

In [Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria "Bulgaria"), Jehovah's Witnesses have been targets of violence by right-wing nationalist groups such as the [IMRO – Bulgarian National Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMRO_%E2%80%93_Bulgarian_National_Movement "IMRO – Bulgarian National Movement"). On April 17, 2011, a group of about sixty hooded men besieged a [Kingdom Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_Hall "Kingdom Hall") in [Burgas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas "Burgas"), during the annual [memorial of Christ's death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorial_of_Christ%27s_death "Memorial of Christ's death"). Attackers threw stones, damaged furniture, and injured at least five of the people gathered inside.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-9)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-10) The incident was recorded by a local television station.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-11) Jehovah's Witnesses in Bulgaria have been fined for proselytizing without proper government permits, and some municipalities have legislation prohibiting or restricting their rights to preach.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-12)

In 1984, Canada released a number of previously classified documents which revealed that in the 1940s, "able bodied young Jehovah's Witnesses" were sent to "camps", and "entire families who practiced the religion were imprisoned".[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-canww2-4) The 1984 report stated, "Recently declassified wartime documents suggest \[World War II\] was also a time of officially sanctioned religious bigotry, political intolerance and the suppression of ideas. The federal government described Jehovah's Witnesses as subversive and offensive 'religious zealots' … in secret reports given to special parliamentarian committees in 1942." It concluded that, "probably no other organization is so offensive in its methods, working as it does under the guise of Christianity. The documents prepared by the justice department were presented to a special House of Commons committee by the government of [William Lyon Mackenzie King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Lyon_Mackenzie_King "William Lyon Mackenzie King") in an attempt to justify the outlawing of the organizations during the second world war."[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-13)

Jehovah's Witnesses' activities in China are considered illegal. Former Canadian-American Jehovah's Witness missionary [Amber Scorah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amber_Scorah "Amber Scorah") recounted the lengths that she and her husband went through to preach illegally in China in the early 2000s. She describes how local Jehovah's Witnesses were forced to meet secretly in a different location every week, with invites by word-of-mouth only.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-14)[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-15) She also describes how they would vet potential converts to make sure they had no Communist ties or leanings.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-16)[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-17)

Under [Fidel Castro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fidel_Castro "Fidel Castro")'s communist regime, Jehovah's Witnesses were included among groups considered to be "social deviants" and were sent to [forced labor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forced_labor "Forced labor") [concentration camps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concentration_camps "Concentration camps") to be "reeducated".[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-18) On July 1, 1974 the group was officially banned and their places of worship closed. Following the ban, members who refused military service were imprisoned for three years; it was reported that members were also imprisoned because of their children's refusal to salute the flag.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-19)

In [Eritrea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eritrea "Eritrea"), the government stripped Jehovah's Witnesses of their civil and political rights in 1994 after their refusal to engage in voting and military service.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-20)[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-21)[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-22) Members of all ages have been arrested for participating in religious meetings.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-23)[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-24) On 24 September 1994, three members were arrested and imprisoned without trial.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-25)[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-Eritrea20-26)[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-27) International rights groups are aware of the situation of Jehovah's Witnesses in Eritrea[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-Eritrea20-26) and have repeatedly called for Eritrean authorities to end the persecution.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-28)

As of July 2016, 55 members were imprisoned.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-29) According to the Watch Tower Society, 28 members were released on December 4, 2020,[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-30) and another four were released in early 2021.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-31)[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-32)

Prior to [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), the French government banned the _[Association of Jehovah's Witnesses in France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporations_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#Corporations_outside_the_United_States "Corporations of Jehovah's Witnesses")_, and ordered that the French offices of the [Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watch_Tower_Bible_and_Tract_Society_of_Pennsylvania "Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society of Pennsylvania") be vacated.[\[Note 1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-34) After the war, Jehovah's Witnesses in France renewed their operations. In December 1952, France's [Minister of the Interior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_the_Interior "Minister of the Interior") banned _[The Watchtower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Watchtower "The Watchtower")_ magazine, citing its position on [military service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_service "Military service").[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-35) The ban was lifted on November 26, 1974.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-36)[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-37)

In the 1990s and 2000s, the French government included Jehovah's Witnesses on its list of "[cults](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cult "Cult")", and governmental ministers made derogatory public statements about Jehovah's Witnesses.[\[Note 2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-39) Despite a century of activity in the country, France's Ministry of Finance opposed official recognition of the denomination; it was not until June 23, 2000 that France's highest administrative court, the Council of State, ruled that Jehovah's Witnesses qualify as a religion under French law.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-40) France's [Ministry of the Interior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_the_Interior "Ministry of the Interior") sought to collect 60% of donations made to the denomination's entities; Witnesses called the taxation "confiscatory" and appealed to the [European Court of Human Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Court_of_Human_Rights "European Court of Human Rights").[\[Note 3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-42)[\[Note 4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-44) On June 30, 2011, the European Court of Human Rights ruled that France's actions violated the religious freedom of Jehovah's Witnesses.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-45)

Jehovah's Witnesses in France have reported hundreds of criminal attacks against their adherents and places of worship.[\[Note 5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-46)

#### French dependencies

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: French dependencies")\]

During the ban of _The Watchtower_ in France, publication of the magazine continued in various French territories. In [French Polynesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Polynesia "French Polynesia"), the magazine was covertly published under the name, _La Sentinelle_, though it was later learned that _The Watchtower_ had not been banned locally.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-47) In [Réunion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R%C3%A9union "Réunion"), the magazine was published under the name, _Bulletin intérieur_.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-48)

In 1996, a year after [Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_/(country/) "Georgia (country)") adopted its [post-USSR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Soviet_Union_/(1985%E2%80%931991/)#Dissolution_of_the_USSR "History of the Soviet Union (1985–1991)") [Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Georgia_/(country/) "Constitution of Georgia (country)"),[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-49) the country's [Ministry of Internal Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Internal_Affairs "Ministry of Internal Affairs") began a campaign to confiscate religious literature belonging to Jehovah's Witnesses.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-50)[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-51) Individual Witnesses fled Georgia seeking religious refugee status in other nations.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-52) Government officials refused permits for Jehovah's Witnesses to organize assemblies, and law enforcement officials dispersed legal assemblies. In September 2000, "Georgian police and security officials fired blank anti-tank shells and used force to disperse an outdoor gathering of some 700 Jehovah's Witnesses in the town of Natuliki in northwestern Georgia on 8 September, AP and Caucasus Press reported."[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-53) In 2002, prosecution of a priest who instigated violence against Jehovah's Witness members was impeded by a lack of cooperation by government and law enforcement.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-54)

In 2004, [Forum 18](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Forum_18_News_Service&action=edit&redlink=1 "Forum 18 News Service (page does not exist)") referred to the period since 1999 as a "five-year reign of terror" against Jehovah's Witnesses and other religious minorities.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-55) [Amnesty International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amnesty_International "Amnesty International") noted: "Jehovah's Witnesses have frequently been a target for violence … in Georgia … In many of the incidents police are said to have failed to protect the believers, or even to have participated in physical and verbal abuse."[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-56)

On May 3, 2007, the [European Court of Human Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Court_of_Human_Rights "European Court of Human Rights") ruled against the government of Georgia for its toleration of religious violence toward Jehovah's Witnesses and ordered the victims be compensated for moral damages and legal costs.[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-57)[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-58)[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-59) On October 7, 2014, the European Court of Human Rights, giving its judgement concerning violence against Jehovah's Witnesses in Georgia in the years 2000–2001, unanimously held that Georgia's state officials, in violation of Articles 3, 9 & 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights, had either directly participated in those attacks or had tolerated violence by private individuals against members of the religious group.[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-60)

In July 2017, the Supreme Court of [South Ossetia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Ossetia "South Ossetia") ruled that Jehovah's Witnesses were an extreme organization. The court declared a penalty of ten years' imprisonment for "any religious activities such as assembly and distributing literature".[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-61)[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-62)

During 1931 and 1932, more than 2000 legal actions were instigated against Jehovah's Witnesses in Germany and members of the group were dismissed from employment.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-63) Persecution intensified following [Adolf Hitler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Hitler "Adolf Hitler")'s appointment as chancellor in 1933 and continued until 1945.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-64) A "[Declaration of Facts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Declaration_of_Facts "Declaration of Facts")" was issued at a Jehovah's Witness convention in Berlin on June 25, 1933, asserting the group's political neutrality and calling for an end to government opposition. More than 2.1 million copies of the statement were distributed throughout Germany,[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-apocalypse-65) but its distribution prompted a new wave of persecution against members of the denomination in Germany, whose refusal to give the [Nazi salute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_salute "Nazi salute"), join Nazi organizations or perform military service demonstrated their opposition to the totalitarian ideology of [National Socialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Socialism "National Socialism").[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-66)

On October 4, 1934, congregations of Jehovah's Witnesses in Germany sent telegrams of protest and warning to Hitler. The Watch Tower Society reported that according to [Karl R. A. Wittig](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Karl_R._A._Wittig&action=edit&redlink=1 "Karl R. A. Wittig (page does not exist)"), a government officer in Germany at the time, Hitler was shown a number of telegrams protesting the Third Reich's persecution of the Bible Students. Wittig reported: "Hitler jumped to his feet and with clenched fists hysterically screamed: 'This brood will be exterminated in Germany!' Four years after this discussion I was able, by my own observations, to convince myself … that Hitler's outburst of anger was not just an idle threat. No other group of prisoners of the named concentration-camps was exposed to the sadism of the SS-soldiery in such a fashion as the Bible Students were. It was a sadism marked by an unending chain of physical and mental tortures, the likes of which no language in the world can express."[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-67)[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-68)

About 10,000 Witnesses were imprisoned, including 2000 sent to [concentration camps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concentration_camps "Concentration camps"), where they were identified by [purple triangles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purple_triangle "Purple triangle"); as many as 1200 died, including 250 who were executed.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-69)[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-70) From 1935 Gestapo officers offered members a document to sign indicating renouncement of their faith, submission to state authority, and support of the German military. Historian Detlef Garbe says a "relatively high number" of people signed the statement before the war, but "extremely low numbers" of Bible Student prisoners did so in concentration camps in later years.[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-71)

After a short, unstable period after WWII, the Witnesses continued to suffer severe persecution in the German Democratic Republic (GDR). The Potsdam Agreement of 1945 guaranteed religious freedom and respect for organizations,[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-72) which also applied to East Germany. When the GDR was established in 1949, the [Constitution of East Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_East_Germany "Constitution of East Germany") included similar guarantees for the practice of religion. However it became clear that these promises were symbolic and had little impact on the ruling authorities' policies. The government restricted the activities of the Protestant and Catholic Churches and banned several smaller religious groups. The Jehovah's Witnesses were subject to the harshest and most prolonged persecution.[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-73) According to the official Jehovah's Witnesses webpage,

> "Congregation meetings were again broken up by the police. Literature was confiscated. Roads were blockaded to prevent the Witnesses from attending a convention. Brothers were arrested. On August 31, 1950, an official ban was imposed. The Witnesses in East Germany were again forced underground, this time by a Communist regime, not to emerge until almost 40 years later."[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-:2-74)

According to Mike Dennis, the main agent of "control surveillance and persecution was the Ministry of State Security, popularly known as the Stasi." Its "mission was to serve as the shield and sword of the SED and to protect the socialist system and the East German state from internal and external threats, especially by uncovering and forestalling 'the hostile plans of the aggressive imperialists and their helpers."[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-75) The Jehovah's Witness website says that in total almost 5,000 Witnesses were imprisoned in 231 places.[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-:2-74)[\[2\]](https://wol.jw.org/en/wol/d/r1/lp-e/301999000?q=germany+nazi&p=par.) Hans-Hermann Dirksen mentions that there were many reasons why this group was persecuted, but primarily because the German Democratic Republic saw their religious activities as "detrimental to their political activities."[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-:1-76) Because the group remained neutral, the SED saw the group as "dangerous and among the enemies of socialism."[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-:1-76) Trials were conducted against the Witnesses because their activities "were deemed as unconstitutional and their investigations proved they were disguised as espionage." The Stasi then proceeded to use new methods to create insecurity within the organization by infiltrating the group in the 1960s.[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-:1-76) Another reason they were persecuted was because the organization's headquarters were in the United States, an enemy of the GDR. The organization remained faithful and continued its service throughout the decades of persecution. It was their "solidarity as a community which enabled them to withstand, often with great stoicism, decomposition and liquidation measures."[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-:1-76)

Despite more than a century of conspicuous activity in the country, Jehovah's Witnesses in Germany were not granted legal recognition until March 25, 2005, in Berlin;[\[Note 6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-78) in 2006 [Germany's Federal Administrative Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Administrative_Court_of_Germany "Federal Administrative Court of Germany") in [Leipzig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leipzig "Leipzig") extended the local decision to apply nationwide.[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-79)

Jehovah's Witnesses' Office of Public Information has documented a number of mob attacks in India.[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-80) It states that these instances of violence "reveal the country's hostility toward its own citizens who are Christians."[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-81)\[_[failed verification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_\] There have been reports that police assist mob attacks on Jehovah's Witnesses or lay charges against the Witnesses while failing to charge other participants involved.[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-82)

In [Davangere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davangere "Davangere") on December 20, 2010 a mob confronted two female Witnesses. The mob broke into the home of one of the Witnesses where they had taken refuge. Property was damaged and one of the Witnesses was assaulted. When the police arrived, the Witnesses were arrested and charged with blasphemy.[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-83)\[_[failed verification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_\] In another incident on December 6, 2011, three Witnesses were attacked by a mob in [Madikeri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madikeri "Madikeri").[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-84)\[_[failed verification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_\] The male Witness "was kicked and pummeled by the mob" and then dragged towards a nearby temple; while making lewd remarks, the mob "tried to tear the clothes off of the female Witnesses". According to the Watch Tower Society, the police "took the three Witnesses to the police station and filed charges against them rather than the mob".[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-85)\[_[failed verification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_\] During a July 2012 incident, a group of fifteen men assaulted four Witnesses in Madikeri. The group was taken to a police station and charged with "insulting the religion or religious beliefs of another class" before being released on bail.[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-86)

In October 2023, [a bomb blast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Kerala_bombing "2023 Kerala bombing") at a Jehovah's Witnesses annual convention in [Kerala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala "Kerala") killed 7 people and injured 50 others. The suspect claimed to be a disillusioned member of the Jehovah's Witnesses, and said he resented the Witnesses' anti-national doctrines.[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-Hindu-87)[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-:0-88)[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-89)

Jehovah's Witnesses' activities in Kazakhstan were banned until 1997.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-90) After the ban was lifted, members continued to experience police disruption and imprisonment.[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-91)[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-92)[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-93) Their activities are currently registered only in some regions of Kazakhstan, and the Watch Tower Society reports that the use of their literature is restricted.[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-94)[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-95)

In 1967, thousands of Jehovah's Witnesses in [Malawi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malawi "Malawi") were beaten and killed, houses and gathering places where burned along with their bibles and publications by police and citizens for refusing to purchase a card indicating endorsement of the [Malawi Congress Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malawi_Congress_Party "Malawi Congress Party").[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-96) While their political neutrality during the time of the old Colonial government was seen as an act of resistance, their continued non-involvement with the new independent government was viewed as treasonous.[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-97) The organization was declared illegal and foreign members in the country were expelled. Persecution, both economic and physical, intensified after a September 1972 Malawi Congress Party meeting which stated that "all Witnesses should be dismissed from their employment; any firm that failed to comply would have its license cancelled". By November 1973, 21,000 Jehovah's Witnesses had fled to neighboring [Zambia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zambia "Zambia").[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-98)[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-99) In 1993, during the transition to a multiparty system and a change in leadership, the government's ban on the organization was lifted.[\[94\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-100)[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-101)[\[96\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-102)

In 2004, the Moscow City Court banned the activities of Jehovah's Witnesses in [Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow "Moscow") and their legal entity was liquidated.[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-103) Russian anti-extremism laws were extended to non-violent groups in 2007 and Jehovah's Witnesses were banned in the port city of [Taganrog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taganrog "Taganrog") in 2009 after a local court ruled that the organization was guilty of inciting religious hatred by "propagating the exclusivity and supremacy" of their religious beliefs.[\[98\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-beard-104) In December 2009, the Supreme Court of Russia upheld the ruling of the lower courts which pronounced 34 pieces of Jehovah's Witness literature extremist, such as their magazine _[The Watchtower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Watchtower "The Watchtower")_.[\[99\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-105) The ruling upheld the confiscation of property of Jehovah's Witnesses in Taganrog. In December 2015, a Rostov Regional Court [convicted 16 Jehovah's Witnesses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trial_of_the_Sixteen_/(2011%E2%80%932015/) "Trial of the Sixteen (2011–2015)") of practicing extremism in Taganrog, with five given 5+1⁄2\-year [suspended sentences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suspended_sentence "Suspended sentence") and the remainder were issued fines they were not required to pay.[\[98\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-beard-104)

In July 2015, the Russian Federation Ministry of Justice added Jehovah's Witnesses' official website to the [Federal List of Extremist Materials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_List_of_Extremist_Materials "Federal List of Extremist Materials"), making it a criminal offense to promote the website from within the country and requiring internet providers throughout Russia to block access to the site.[\[100\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-106) In March 2017, the [Russian News Agency TASS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_News_Agency_TASS "Russian News Agency TASS") reported that Russia's Justice Ministry had suspended the activities of the Administrative Center of Jehovah's Witnesses in Russia due to extremist activities.[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-107) In April 2017, [UN Special Rapporteur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UN_Special_Rapporteur "UN Special Rapporteur") on Freedom of Opinion and Expression [David Kaye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Kaye_/(voice_actor/) "David Kaye (voice actor)"), UN Special Rapporteur on Freedoms of Peaceful Assembly and Association [Maina Kiai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maina_Kiai "Maina Kiai"), and UN Special Rapporteur on Freedom of Religion and Belief [Ahmed Shaheed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmed_Shaheed "Ahmed Shaheed") condemned Russia's desire to ban Jehovah's Witnesses.[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-auto-108)

On April 20, 2017, The [Supreme Court of Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_Russia "Supreme Court of Russia") issued a verdict upholding the claim from the country's Justice Ministry that Jehovah's Witnesses' activity violated laws on "extremism". The ruling liquidated the group's Russian headquarters in [Saint Petersburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Petersburg "Saint Petersburg") and all of its 395 local religious organizations, banning their activity and ordering their property to be seized by the state. According to the human rights organization Forum 18, this is the first time a court has ruled a registered national centralized religious organization as "extremist".[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-auto-108)[\[103\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-109) Many countries and international organizations have spoken out against Russia's religious abuses of Jehovah's Witnesses.[\[104\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-110)[\[105\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-111)[\[106\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-112) Leaders of various denominations have also spoken out against Russia's decision to ban the denomination.[\[107\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-113)[\[108\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-114)[\[109\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-115)[\[110\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-116) An article in _[Newsweek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newsweek "Newsweek")_ stated, "Russia's decision to ban Jehovah's Witnesses in the country shows the 'paranoia' of Vladimir Putin's government, according to the chair of the [United States Commission on International Religious Freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Commission_on_International_Religious_Freedom "United States Commission on International Religious Freedom") (USCIRF)."[\[111\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-117) The [United States Holocaust Memorial Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Holocaust_Memorial_Museum "United States Holocaust Memorial Museum") also expressed deep concern over Russia's treatment of Jehovah's Witnesses.[\[112\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-118)

In May 2017, armed Federal Security Services (FSB) officers arrested Dennis Christensen, a 46-year-old Danish citizen, at a hall in [Oryol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oryol "Oryol") on charges related to extremism.[\[113\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-119)[\[114\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-120) On February 6, 2019, he was found guilty and sentenced to six years in prison.[\[115\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-121)

A 2019 arrest in [Surgut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surgut "Surgut") of a Jehovah's Witness has been alleged to involve torture.[\[116\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-122)

In February 2021, a Russian court in the [Republic of Khakassia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khakassia "Khakassia") sentenced 69-year-old Valentina Baranovskaya to two years in prison for taking part in religious activities that have been banned in Russia. She is the first female member of the denomination to be imprisoned in Russia since their activities were banned in 2017. Her 46-year-old son Roman Baranovsky was also sentenced to six years in prison.[\[117\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-123)[\[118\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-124) According to the Watch Tower Society, the Supreme Court denied their appeal on May 24, 2021, and added restrictions to be imposed on them after their release.[\[119\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-125) Commenting on the sentence, the [USCIRF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Commission_on_International_Religious_Freedom "United States Commission on International Religious Freedom") tweeted that the sentencing of an elderly woman in poor health marks a "new low in Russia's brutal campaign against religious freedom."[\[120\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-126)

In October 2022, three Jehovah's Witnesses were sentenced to six years in prison in [Sevastopol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sevastopol "Sevastopol") after the Ukrainian city was annexed by Russia in 2014. Although the denomination's activities are legal in Ukraine, the decision was made by "a Moscow-imposed court" that found them guilty of organizing activities for Jehovah's Witnesses.[\[121\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-127)

In 1972, the [Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singapore "Singapore") government de-registered and banned the activities of Jehovah's Witnesses on the grounds that its members refuse to perform military service (which is obligatory for all male citizens), salute [the flag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flag_of_Singapore "Flag of Singapore"), or swear oaths of allegiance to the state.[\[122\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-state.gov-128)[\[123\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-129) Literature published by the denomination was also banned, and a person in possession of the banned literature may be fined up to S$2,000 (US$1,333) and jailed up to 12 months for a first conviction.[\[124\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-130)

In 1994, the [High Court of Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Court_of_Singapore "High Court of Singapore") ruled on the case of _[Chan Hiang Leng Colin v Public Prosecutor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chan_Hiang_Leng_Colin_v_Public_Prosecutor "Chan Hiang Leng Colin v Public Prosecutor")_, finding that banning the Jehovah's Witnesses did not violate the right to [freedom of religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Singapore "Freedom of religion in Singapore") guaranteed by [Article 15(1)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Article_15_of_the_Constitution_of_Singapore "Article 15 of the Constitution of Singapore") of the [Constitution of Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Singapore "Constitution of Singapore"). According to the ruling by Chief Justice [Yong Pung How](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yong_Pung_How "Yong Pung How"), their refusal to perform military service was contrary to public peace, welfare and good order, and laws relating to public order are exceptions to freedom of religion set out in Article 15(4).[\[125\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-131)

In February 1995, Singapore police raided private homes where group members were holding religious meetings, in an operation codenamed "Operation Hope". Officers seized Bibles, religious literature, documents and computers, and eventually brought charges against 69 Jehovah's Witnesses, many of whom went to jail.[\[126\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-singapore-window.org-132)[\[127\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-133) In March 1995, 74-year-old Yu Nguk Ding was arrested for carrying two "undesirable publications"—one of them a Bible printed by the Watch Tower Society.[\[128\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-134)

In 1996, eighteen Jehovah's Witnesses were convicted for unlawfully meeting in a Singapore apartment and were given sentences from one to four weeks in jail.[\[129\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-135) [Canadian Queen's Counsel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen%27s_Counsel#Canada "Queen's Counsel") Glen How argued that the restrictions against the Jehovah's Witnesses violated their constitutional rights. Then-Chief Justice [Yong Pung How](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yong_Pung_How "Yong Pung How") questioned How's sanity, accused him of "living in a cartoon world" and referred to "funny, cranky religious groups" before denying the appeal.[\[126\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-singapore-window.org-132) In 1998, two Jehovah's Witnesses were charged in a Singapore court for possessing and distributing banned religious publications.[\[130\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-136)

In 1998, a Jehovah's Witness lost a lawsuit against a government school for wrongful dismissal for refusing to sing the [national anthem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Majulah_Singapura "Majulah Singapura") or salute the flag. In March 1999, the Court of Appeals denied his appeal.[\[122\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-state.gov-128) In 2000, public secondary schools indefinitely suspended at least fifteen Jehovah's Witness students for refusing to sing the national anthem or participate in the flag ceremony.[\[131\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-ReferenceA-137) In April 2001, one public school teacher, also a member of Jehovah's Witnesses, resigned after being threatened with dismissal for refusing to participate in singing the national anthem.[\[122\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-state.gov-128)

Singapore authorities have seized Jehovah's Witnesses' literature on various occasions from individuals attempting to cross the [Malaysia–Singapore border](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaysia%E2%80%93Singapore_border "Malaysia–Singapore border"). In thirteen cases, authorities warned the Jehovah's Witnesses but did not press charges.[\[131\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-ReferenceA-137)[\[132\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-138)[\[133\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-ReferenceB-139)

The initial sentence for failure to comply is 15 months' imprisonment, with an additional 24 months for a second refusal. Failure to perform annual military reserve duty, which is required of all those who have completed their initial two-year obligation, results in a 40-day sentence, with a 12-month sentence after four refusals.[\[133\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-ReferenceB-139)[\[134\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-140)

Beginning on June 7, 1967, the [apartheid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apartheid "Apartheid") South African government passed the Defense Amendment Bill, making it compulsory for all white males of eligible age to participate in the armed forces.[\[135\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-141) Conscription brought Jehovah's Witnesses into conflict with the government, and young men who refused military service were sentenced to no less than 12 months at a military detention barracks, with repeat convictions in some cases. According to the Survey of Race Relations in South Africa of 1974, during 1973, 158 Jehovah's Witnesses were sentenced "for refusing on religious grounds to render service or undergo training." In the first half of 1974, 120 Jehovah's Witnesses were sentenced.[\[136\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-142) Conscription was officially ended in late August 1993. By this time, the Constitution of South Africa had been adjusted to allow for [alternative civilian service instead of military service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/End_Conscription_Campaign "End Conscription Campaign").

Jehovah's Witnesses did not have a significant presence in the Soviet Union prior to 1939 when the Soviet Union incorporated eastern Romania, [Moldavia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldavia "Moldavia"), and [Lithuania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithuania "Lithuania"), each of which had a Jehovah's Witness movement. Although never large in number (estimated by the [KGB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KGB "KGB") to be 20,000 in 1968), the Jehovah's Witnesses became one of the most persecuted religious groups in the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union") during the post-World War II era.[\[137\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-143) Members were arrested or deported, and some were put in labor camps. Witnesses in [Moldavian SSR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldavian_SSR "Moldavian SSR") were deported to [Tomsk Oblast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomsk_Oblast "Tomsk Oblast"); members from other regions of the Soviet Union were deported to [Irkutsk Oblast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irkutsk_Oblast "Irkutsk Oblast").[\[138\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-polian-144) KGB officials, who were tasked with dissolving the Jehovah's Witness movement, were disturbed to discover that the Witnesses continued to practice their faith even within the labor camps.[\[139\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-145)

The Minister of Internal Affairs, [Viktor Semyonovich Abakumov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viktor_Semyonovich_Abakumov "Viktor Semyonovich Abakumov") proposed the deportation of the Jehovah's Witnesses to Stalin in October 1950. A resolution was voted by the Council of Minister and an order was issued by the [Ministry for State Security](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_for_State_Security_/(USSR/) "Ministry for State Security (USSR)") in March 1951. The [Moldavian SSR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldavian_SSR "Moldavian SSR") passed a decree "on the confiscation and selling of the property of individuals banished from the territory of the Moldavian SSR", which included the Jehovah's Witnesses.[\[138\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-polian-144)

In April 1951, over 9,000 Jehovah's Witnesses were deported to [Siberia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siberia "Siberia") under a plan called "[Operation North](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_North "Operation North")".[\[140\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-146)[\[141\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-passat-147) The Soviet government was so disturbed by the Jehovah's Witnesses who continued to receive religious literature smuggled from Brooklyn that the KGB was authorized to send agents to infiltrate the Brooklyn headquarters.[\[142\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-148)

In September 1965, a decree of the Presidium of the [USSR Council of Ministers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USSR_Council_of_Ministers "USSR Council of Ministers") canceled the "special settlement" restriction of Jehovah's Witnesses, though the decree, signed by [Anastas Mikoyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anastas_Mikoyan "Anastas Mikoyan"), stated that there would be no compensation for confiscated property. However, Jehovah's Witnesses remained the subject of state persecution due to their ideology being classified as [anti-Soviet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-Soviet "Anti-Soviet").[\[143\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-kphg-149)

The [United Nations Human Rights Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Human_Rights_Committee "United Nations Human Rights Committee") has indicated that Jehovah's Witnesses in Turkmenistan have been prosecuted and imprisoned for refusing to perform compulsory military service, despite Turkmenistan's constitution guaranteeing the right to "practice any religion alone or in association with others" and the right to "freedom of conviction and the free expression of those convictions". The UN committee noted, "The State party should take all necessary measures to review its legislation with a view to providing for alternative military service. The State party should also ensure that the law clearly stipulates that individuals have the right to conscientious objection to military service. Furthermore, the State party should halt all prosecutions of individuals who refuse to perform military service on grounds of conscience and release those individuals who are currently serving prison sentences."[\[144\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-ohchr-_turkmenistan-150) In May 2021, the Watch Tower Society reported that Turkmenistan has released all Jehovah's Witnesses who had been imprisoned for conscientious objection to military service.[\[145\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-151)

According to the [US Department of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_State "United States Department of State"), [Turkmenistan's Ministry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_Ministers_/(Turkmenistan/) "Cabinet of Ministers (Turkmenistan)") of Justice described Jehovah's Witnesses as foreign and dangerous. The US State Department also stated that the Turkmenistan government imposes restrictions on the freedom of Jehovah's Witness parents (and members of various other religious groups) to raise their children in accordance with their religious beliefs. In 2003, Jehovah's Witnesses' religious literature was confiscated, members of the denomination were denied exit visas, and others were stopped after crossing a border and forced to return. In 2004, five Jehovah's Witnesses were stopped and prevented from boarding a flight to another country because their names were included on a "black list" of citizens prohibited from leaving the country.[\[146\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-152) In 2015, a Jehovah's Witness in Turkmenistan was sentenced to four years in prison for allegedly inciting hatred at a religious meeting held in a private home, and other attendees were fined.[\[147\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-153)[\[148\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-154)[\[149\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-155)

During the 1930s and 1940s, some US states passed laws that made it illegal for Jehovah's Witnesses to distribute their literature, and children of Jehovah's Witnesses in some states were banned from attending [state schools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_school "State school").

The persecution of Jehovah's Witnesses for their refusal to salute the flag became known as the "Flag-Salute Cases".[\[150\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-156) Their refusal to salute the flag became considered as a test of the liberties for which the flag stands, namely the freedom to worship according to the dictates of one's own conscience. The [Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Supreme Court of the United States") found that the United States, by making the flag salute compulsory in _[Minersville School District v. Gobitis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minersville_School_District_v._Gobitis "Minersville School District v. Gobitis")_ (1940), was impinging upon the individual's right to worship as one chooses—a violation of the First Amendment Free Exercise Clause in the constitution. However, Justice Frankfurter, speaking on behalf of the 8-to-1 majority view against the Witnesses, stated that the interests of "inculcating patriotism was of sufficient importance to justify a relatively minor infringement on religious belief".[\[151\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-Hall_395-157) The ruling resulted in a wave of persecution. Lillian Gobitas, one of the schoolchildren involved in the decision, said, "It was like open season on Jehovah's Witnesses."[\[152\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-158)

The [American Civil Liberties Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_Liberties_Union "American Civil Liberties Union") reported that by the end of 1940, "more than 1,500 Witnesses in the United States had been victimized in 335 separate attacks".[\[153\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-159) Such attacks included beatings, being tarred and feathered, hanged, shot, maimed, and even castrated.[\[154\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-160) As reports of attacks against Jehovah's Witnesses continued, "several justices changed their minds, and in _[West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Virginia_State_Board_of_Education_v._Barnette "West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette")_ (1943), the Court declared that the state could not impinge on the First Amendment by compelling the observance of rituals."[\[151\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-Hall_395-157)

In 1943, after a drawn-out litigation process by the [Watch Tower Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watch_Tower_Society "Watch Tower Society") in state courts and lower federal courts, the Supreme Court ruled that public school officials could not force Jehovah's Witnesses and other students to salute the flag and recite the [Pledge of Allegiance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pledge_of_Allegiance_/(United_States/) "Pledge of Allegiance (United States)").[\[155\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-161) In 1946 and 1953 Supreme Court decisions were handed down establishing their right to be exempted from military service.[\[156\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-162)[\[157\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-163)[\[158\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-164)[\[159\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Jehovah%27s_Witnesses#cite_note-165)

Charles Taze Russell (1852-1916) is regarded as the originator of the Bible
Student movement of the late 19 th century in the United States (US). Russell
believed that traditional churches had abandoned the faith of the ‘primitive
church’, and that the restoration of true Christianity could be achieved through a
more literal reading of the Bible and a sincere devotion to following its teachings.
The Bible Student movement spawned several independent student associations,
including one which would later become the Jehovah’s Witnesses.

Jehovah's Witnesses take their name from what was once believed to be the holy
name of God referenced in the Hebrew Bible. In the 19 th century ‘Jehovah’ was
thought to be the pronunciation of YHWH or JHVH, an English transliteration of
the divine name which appears frequently in the Old Testament. Joining this term


Human Rights Without Frontiers Int’l 1


with a passage from the prophet Isaiah - ‘You are my witnesses that I am God’
(43:12) - the organisation eventually became known as Jehovah’s Witnesses.

Jehovah’s Witnesses are now present in 240 countries and territories, with a
worldwide membership of more than 8.2 million evangelists. In Europe, there are
more than 16,000 congregations and 1.5 million active members.

Jehovah’s Witnesses are especially known for their door-to-door evangelism and
the wide distribution of the group’s literature, notably _The Watchtower_ magazine
and _Awake!_ . Attendance at their conventions can reach more than 15 million, with
[nearly 20 million attending the denomination’s annual Memorial observing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jehovah%27s_Witnesses_practices#Memorial_of_Christ.27s_death)
Christ’s death.

Jehovah's Witnesses are directed by its Governing Body, which is based in New
[York City in the US and establishes all doctrines and interpretations of the Bible.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bible)
They prefer to use their own translation, which they call the _[New World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_World_Translation_of_the_Holy_Scriptures)_
_[Translation of the Holy Scriptures.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_World_Translation_of_the_Holy_Scriptures)_

Since their establishment, Jehovah’s Witnesses have been repressed by several
governments, most notably:


  the Nazi regime in Germany and in countries under Nazi control between

1933 and 1945. They were sent to concentration camps and sentenced to
death, sometimes by decapitation;

  Communist regimes between 1917 and 1989;

  the fascist regimes in Spain and Portugal until the 1970s;

  and the imperial regime of Japan and other dictatorships.

Most recently, the movement of Jehovah’s Witnesses was banned in Russia in
2018 and dozens of them are now in prison.

Jehovah’s Witnesses are mostly imprisoned for their refusal to perform military
service in countries where there is no alternative civilian service, for sharing their
beliefs in the public space, and for proselytising.

Where there are victims of arrests, prison sentences and discrimination, Jehovah’s
Witnesses will actively litigate to protect their members. This has helped shape
jurisprudence related to freedom of religion or belief in many countries
throughout the world.

**Teachings**


Consistent with its origins in the teachings of Charles Taze Russell, Jehovah’s
Witnesses claim to recover the truths of the ‘primitive church’. They place special
emphasis on the Second Coming of Christ and the final judgement of those who
reject his message. They believe that one day the earth will be destroyed, and then
Paradise will be restored according to God’s plan for creation.

The Jehovah’s Witnesses adhere to several distinctive doctrines and practices that
differ significantly from those of the majority of Christians. For example, they
reject the Orthodox Christian belief in the Trinity and refuse to observe traditional
Christian holidays, such as Christmas and Easter, which they consider to be of
pagan origins or otherwise incompatible with the Christian faith.

Jehovah’s Witnesses are generally moderate in their lifestyle and refrain from
smoking, the abuse of alcohol, and sexual relations outside of marriage. They
strive to be good citizens, respectful toward authorities, and law-abiding, except
in cases where the law conflicts with their conscience as Christians.


**ERITREA: Reasons for the Persecution of Jehovah’s Witnesses**

According to July 2018 estimates by the US government, the total population of
Eritrea is six million. There are no reliable figures on religious affiliation, but it

1
is estimated that 49% of the population are Christian and 49% are Sunni Muslim.

The country is ruled by a totalitarian one-party dictatorship of Maoist inspiration.
Eritrea gained independence from Ethiopia in 1991 after 30 years of continuous
armed struggle by the Eritrean Liberation Front. Since then, national presidential
or legislative elections have never taken place.

A number of beliefs and practices of Jehovah’s Witnesses have been perceived
negatively by the current government.

Jehovah’s Witnesses are politically neutral and conscientiously cannot participate
in military service. They refuse to kill or receive training on how to kill. Because
they will not participate in compulsory military service, Eritrean authorities
consider them to be opposed to the regime.

**RUSSIA: Reasons for the Persecution of Jehovah’s Witnesses**

As of July 2018, the US government estimated the total population of Russia to be
142.2 million. A 2015-2016 poll by the Pew Research Centre reported that 71% of
the population is Orthodox Christian, while 10% identify as Muslim. 9 According to
the international headquarters of the Jehovah’s Witnesses, their movement in
Russia, which was legalised in 1991, is comprised of 395 local branches and
175,000 members. 10

In April 2017, the Russian Supreme Court banned all Jehovah’s Witnesses
organisations in Russia and confiscated all their properties. It declared the
Jehovah’s Witnesses Administrative Centre, the head office for all 395 branches,
an extremist organisation and ruled that all branches must be shut down.

This ruling was the last stage of an increasingly repressive policy starting in the
early 2000s when the National Security Concept was extended to the spiritual
realm.

The spiritual security concept is closely associated with the persisting Soviet
paranoia of ‘foreign’ enemies and ‘foreign’ ideas. On 20 July 2012, President
Vladimir Putin signed the so-called ‘foreign agent law’ that requires non-profit
organisations that receive foreign funding and allegedly engage in ‘political
activity’ to register and declare themselves as ‘foreign agents’. Russian human
rights NGOs fell into that category and so were forced to stigmatise themselves
publicly. The concept of a ‘foreign agent’ quickly extended to religious
organisations of foreign origin. Concretely, this spiritual security concept resulted
in a religious cleansing policy that targets movements perceived as a threat to the
identity of the Russian people and the Slavic and Orthodox Christian values. The
door was opened to a sacred and natural alliance between the Kremlin and the
Russian Orthodox Church, the main beneficiary of President Putin’s spiritual
security policy.

Simultaneously, the criminalisation of violent extremism progressively evolved
until it included a vague concept of extremism without violence. This was
condemned by the United Nations, the Council of Europe and its Venice
Commission, the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE)
and other transnational institutions. Proselytism became ‘propaganda of
exclusivity, superiority or inferiority of a person on the basis of their religious

The Russian Orthodox Church, the Catholic Church and other mainstream

Buddhism are not targeted by the spiritual security concept and the antiextremism laws. New and dissenting religious movements that are not controlled
by these established religions are the victims of this legislation, especially
Jehovah’s Witnesses.

**CASE STUDIES**


_**Sentenced to 30 months in prison by a court-martial**_


**Brendon Jun Kai Hew** was born on in Singapore, but his family moved to the
state of Sabah in East Malaysia when he was 12 years old. However, his family
decided to return to Singapore in February 2018 so that he could fulfil his national
service obligation as required by law.

When he reported for national service, Brendon Jun Kai Hew was assigned to the
military. Since his conscience would not allow him to perform military service,
he requested alternative civilian service instead. He expressed his wishes to the
officers at the military camp where he was assigned and to the military tribunal
during his court-martial hearings. Despite his repeated requests, he was sentenced
to 30 months’ imprisonment. Brendon Jun Kai Hew is expected to be released on
21 September 2020. 28

other religions, propagandistic books on their religion, which has become

It is apparent that the proselytism activities of Jehovah’s Witnesses and the
reaction of the majority Muslim population are the main justifications for the ban.

**Conclusions**


Jehovah’s Witnesses are not engaged politically and do not pose any security
threat to society in any country worldwide. Generally, they obey the law of the
land and respect authorities. At the same time, like most religious traditions, there
are limits to that obedience. Jehovah’s Witnesses will practice civil disobedience
when laws conflict with their conscience. This has resulted in harassment, fines,
and imprisonment in some countries.

Authorities in countries where Jehovah’s Witnesses are present would do well to
review their legal framework for such groups within their borders. Some
countries have started to do just that. For example, in January 2016, Azerbaijan
released its last two Jehovah’s Witnesses from prison. Kazakhstan freed its last
Jehovah’s Witness in April 2018. In December 2019, South Korea, which had
sentenced over 19,300 Jehovah’s Witnesses to a combined total of 36,000 years
in prison since 1953 as conscientious objectors, set them free and started the
necessary legislative work to provide for an alternative civilian service.

Jehovah’s Witnesses never abandon their members in distress. As a collective,
they try to solve issues with national and local authorities through dialogue. They
have excellent teams of international human rights lawyers who fight for the
release of those who were arrested or sentenced to a prison term or fine. They
combat discrimination and intolerance based on religion in national and supranational courts. They use the mechanisms of the United Nations, the Organisation
for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE), the European Union and other
institutions to remove all obstacles to the exercise of religious freedom. Thus,
they enlarge the space for freedom of religion or belief to other groups in addition
to their members. 45
